speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. My colleague, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) and I will be very shortly beginning a new round of pre-budget consultations.
I cannot overstate the importance that I accord to these meetings. The presentations by representatives of the business, labour, consumer, social and voluntary communities are invaluable to us. They make an indispensable contribution to the decision-making process by achieving better communication between the Government and Canadians, better understanding of the problems facing the country, and better solutions to these problems.
The forthcoming round of consultations will focus on the key elements of the Government's economic strategy. That strategy has had one overriding objective-the renewal and sustained growth of the economy and the creation of jobs for Canadians.

We are succeeding. The economic indicators attest to that. But most important, we have made significant progress in laying the foundation for a more productive, dynamic economy capable of sustaining growth.

Further progress depends on our continuing to build on the strong foundation that we put in place. Our consultation agenda reflects this vitally important continuity and consistency. I want to take this opportunity to set out the agenda for consultation, then I want to deal with tax reform, which is one of the main issues.
The first agenda item is fiscal responsibility. Sound, responsible management of the nation's finances continues to be crucial. If Canadians are to have the full benefit of a more productive and prosperous economy, we must get on with this job. As Members know, we are committed to a fiscal plan that reduces the deficit annually to the end of the decade. I will be seeking the views of Canadians on measures that should be considered to achieve this objective.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Wilson

The second item on our consultations agenda is improving the climate for economic growth and job creation.

Our objective is to encourage and facilitate a continuing improvement in the competitive position of our economy. From the outset our renewal program has recognized the critical importance of a dynamic private sector. Past policies have often obstructed private sector initiative and stifled opportunities for economic development. We have been acting to identify and remove obstacles to private initiative, such as overbearing government regulation, inadequate and shortsighted provisions for training and skill development, and disincentives for investment. At the same time, we have sought opportunities to encourage entrepreneurial activity and to encourage the full participation of young people and women in Canadian economic life. We will continue these important thrusts.
In my last Budget I initiated a review of our major social transfer programs and related tax provisions. I set out four principles to guide that review. As we proceed with that review I will be seeking to develop measures that are consistent with the directions of comprehensive tax reform. In these and other areas, we are relying on the assistance of Canadians to help identify problems and offer solutions.
We will also welcome suggestions on where we might reallocate resources to higher priority areas in order to continue to address these challenges in a fiscally responsible
way.
The third item on the consultations agenda is promoting trade and expanding foreign markets.

Ensuring Canada's stature as a superior world trader is a compelling national imperative. Our economic well-being derives largely from our ability to compete. We must also enhance our access to traditional markets and secure new ones. I am looking forward to the views of business and labour on matters that bear on our ability to compete.

The fourth item for consultation, one that I want to discuss in some detail, is tax reform. Members will recall that on July 18 of this year I announced the Government's intention to proceed with a review of options for comprehensive tax reform.
Tax reform itself is not a new initiative. In the 1984 agenda paper, the Government identified the tax system as an obstacle to growth. In a gradual and measured way over the past two years we have introduced a number of important improvements to the system.
In the area of corporate tax, we have taken steps to broaden the tax base, reduce tax rates, remove investment distorting incentives and simplify the system.
In the area of personal income tax, we have broadened the tax base by eliminating a number of tax avoidance techniques and introduced a minimum tax to ensure that high income people cannot avoid paying any tax.
[ Translation]
And this year I began a detailed examination of a possible replacement for the outdated, unfair and inefficient federal sales tax.

We have made progress, but in considering the further progress we wish to make, and in light of the recent major changes in the United States, we decided that a broader approach to tax reform in Canada is required. Such an approach would consider the system as a whole. It would seek a better balance between personal, corporate and sales taxes, and would make complementary changes in a co-ordinated way. My July 18 announcement signalled that new approach.
Comprehensive tax reform offers Canada an important opportunity to make changes to meet today's realities and to gear up to meet the challenges of the decades to come. We have the opportunity to make the tax system simpler and fairer for all Canadians, to create a tax environment that more effectively encourages productive economic activity and support social justice, and to shape a tax system that meets the national need for a stable source of revenue to finance essential public services. These are the main objectives of tax reform.
The reform effort is being carried out within a number of specific guidelines. The first guideline is fairness. No characteristic of the tax system is more important in the minds of Canadians than fairness.
The Government has already made a start to enhancing the equity of the tax system. We have introduced a minimum personal income tax. We have curtailed tax shelter techniques and eliminated the use of limited partnerships to avoid tax. We halted the practice of income splitting through interest free loans between family members as a means of reducing tax. These are all steps in the right direction, but much more remains to be done.
Clearly, the tax system must ensure the fair sharing of the tax burden among taxpayers. People in similar circumstances should be treated by the tax system in the same way. High-income individuals and profitable corporations should all pay their fair share.
It is our intention to reduce sharply the special tax preferences for individuals and corporations. By doing so we will be able to reduce significantly the rates of personal income tax paid by Canadians, and that will mean higher take-home pay.
We will look at ways of further improving support for low-income Canadians through the tax system. We have already introduced a refundable sales tax credit and prepayment of the child tax credit. Tax reform offers the opportunity to build on these progressive measures.
October 23, 1986

Because the current federal sales tax treats similar products very differently, and because different rates of tax apply to various goods and services, an important part of the over-all tax burden is unevenly distributed through the economy. Similar products should bear the same rate of tax and the sales tax burden should be spread more equally across goods and services.
The second guideline is simplification. It is not difficult to believe that the word Canadians are most likely to associate with the tax system is "complex". The more complex the tax system is, the more likely it is to lose the respect and confidence of most Canadians and thereby to have its effectiveness diminished. A simpler tax system can be achieved on a number of fronts-simpler tax forms, improved tax policies, a broadened tax base and a simpler rate structure. These would result in less need for business and individuals to take tax considerations into account in business and financial decisions.

Tax reform will aim to make the system simpler for small businesses. And it will aim to make compliance easier for individual Canadians. By doing so we will strengthen the selfassessment principle that is the basis of our tax system.
Third, balance. One of the biggest problems in the present tax system is that the amount of personal income tax Canadians are paying is too high.
This excessive reliance on the personal income tax must be halted. The government believes that personal income taxes should be reduced to leave more money in the pockets of Canadians to spend or save as they see fit. This means we will be seeking higher revenues from the corporate and sales tax systems. This will be done in a balanced, fair way.
The fourth guideline is revenue stability. We must ensure that tax reform increases the certainty of achieving the revenue goals the Government sets. A stable and predictable source of revenue is essential to the Government's budgeting process. However, certain features of the corporate and sales tax systems contribute to revenue instability. Such instability makes it difficult to manage the nation's finances responsibly.
Revenue stability can be increased by limiting tax expenditures, reforming the federal sales tax and reducing the need for ad hoc changes in tax rules. Hon. Members are well aware of this Government's commitment to fiscal responsibility. It is the Government's intention to ensure, through a reform of the tax system, a sounder, more predictable revenue base. It is not our intention to take greater revenues. However, while tax reform is proceeding, I cannot preclude other tax action if such action is necessary to meet the goals of fiscal management and economic and social policy.
The fifth guideline is international competitiveness. Earlier I spoke of the necessity of keeping Canada competitive in world
The Address-Mr. Wilson
trade. The tax system should reinforce the ability of Canadians to compete. Given the major changes in the United States, particularly reduced corporate and personal tax rates, we in Canada must ensure that our tax system keeps in step where our competitive position is at stake. The corporate tax system must continue to be conducive to investment. This will maintain and enhance our job creating ability. Because the knowledge, skills and drive of people are the key to a successful modern economy, we must ensure that the tax system is not a deterrent to retaining and attracting key people.
Our sales tax system is also in need of reform to remove the serious competitive biases that currently put our exports at a disadvantage and favour imports.

Sixth, economic growth. Relatively high marginal rates, a narrow base and numerous selective write-offs, deductions and credits have reduced the role of business judgment in shaping investment decisions and made tax considerations far too influential. Such a system does not make for the most efficient allocation of capital.

In pursuing tax reform, we shall intensify our examination of the multitude of tax preferences which have built up over the years. Reducing the number of selected tax preferences, broadening the tax base and lowering tax rates will give market opportunities a greater role in investment decisions. This will result in better prospects for job-producing economic growth and will also mean that lower tax rates will result in a greater incentive for Canadians to work and invest.
A reformed tax system must also recognize distinctively Canadian priorities and values. Tax reform should assist in meeting national, social and economic needs. The tax system must be sensitive to our commitment to build greater regional equality. To help finance our large capital requirements, it must encourage domestic savings. It must continue to support affordable post-secondary education and medical insurance. It must reflect our commitment to social justice by providing effective ways to assist Canadians most in need.
The eighth guideline is measured transition. The implementation of tax reform should not leave Canadians in doubt about tax rules. The Government is committed to a measured transition so that businesses and investors will not need to suspend their long-term planning while changes in the tax system are being discussed. A measured transition will also allow Canadians time to understand the new system and to adjust to it.
A final important guideline is consultation. I reaffirmed at the outset my personal commitment to consultation. Consultation will be especially important for such a far-reaching initiative as comprehensive tax reform. I will be keenly interested in receiving the views of all Canadians in the course of the coming pre-budget consultations. I will also ask for the involvement of Hon. Members in this process and I will be

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Wilson
referring the guidelines and directions set out in the document I am tabling today for review.
[Translation}
I will also consult extensively with my provincial colleagues in an effort to ensure harmonized tax systems across the country.

Fiscal responsibility and tax reform are clearly linked. The options for tax reform would be severely limited if we did not continue our commitment to reduce budget deficits and greater spending control. Through continued expenditure restraint we are creating considerably more flexibility for tax reform.

Today marks the beginning of my new round of pre-budget consultations. The issues I shall be discussing with Canadians are crucial to our nation's continuing ability to provide jobs and prosperity.

As the next step in the tax reform process, I intend to issue specific directions for change at the time of my next Budget. In my November 1984 Economic Statement 1 said we must address the causes of our economic problems and not just the symptoms. It is evident from our record of performance and our plans for building on that performance that we are indeed doing just that.
[ Translation]
Comprehensive tax reform clearly presents an enormous opportunity and an equally major challenge. By reducing the number of tax breaks that benefit only a few, by ensuring that profitable corporations pay their fair share, and by relying more on corporate and sales tax revenues, we will be able to cut personal income tax rates. That means increased take-home pay for Canadians. And the overall result will be a simpler, fairer and more efficient tax system.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to offer some comments and raise some questions with respect to the Minister's remarks.
The Minister spoke of fairness as one of the Government's main objectives in tax reform. This is certainly a worthy goal. However, the actions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) over the past two years strongly suggest that the Government's tax reform will be a sham reform and not a real one. After all, it was his Government which created the new capital gains tax exemption giving higher tax breaks to a handful of wealthy Canadians. On behalf of ordinary Canadians I ask: Is that fair? I think the answer is clear-it is not fair.
In its last two Budgets the Government increased taxes for ordinary Canadians to the point that this year a family with two children and one income-earner earning $30,000 a year will pay $630 more in taxes. I ask again: Is that fair? I think the answer is clear-it is not fair. The Government talks about fairness but its actions have proven that it is moving and will likely continue to move in the opposite direction. One question springs to mind: Will the Government do as the United States has decided to do in its tax reform and fully tax capital gains?
October 23, 1986

The Minister says in his statement that he wants to ensure that "profitable corporations pay their fair share". But how does the Minister and the Government intend to define "profits"? The Government could define them in such a way that many corporations would still escape from paying their fair share of taxes. So I ask the Government: Will it create a minimum tax for corporations?
The Government talks about relying more on sales tax revenues, broadening the sales tax base and cutting personal tax rates so that there will be increased take-home pay for Canadians. Who ultimately pays sales taxes? It is the individual Canadian without regard to level of income and ability to pay. It is clear and well understood that sales taxes are regressive. They are a heavier burden on lower income people. The Government sounds as if it were intending to raise sales tax rates or impose new sales taxes, perhaps called by another name, on goods and transactions, such as the sales of services which are now exempt from sales taxes. If that is what the Government intends to do-and it is giving a very strong signal that it is when it talks about broadening the base for sales taxes-then it is creating a cruel illusion for ordinary Canadians by seeming to put more money into their pockets through the lowering of personal tax rates and then taking money out of those same pockets by making ordinary Canadians pay higher sales taxes. If this happens, and the signal is there in the Minister's speech, then the new Tory tax reform will be nothing but a sham. In fact, if I may say so, it will be nothing but a fraud perpetrated on ordinary Canadians.
The Minister talked about stability as one of his goals. He talked about stability by saying that "raising more total tax revenue is not an objective of tax reform but that it should increase the certainty of achieving the revenue goals that the Government has set for itself'. I ask the Government: Will it be making a commitment right now to rule out any efforts to raise more money through its so-called tax reform? If it does raise more money through this tax reform, will it commit itself to returning the revenues to Canadians through lower taxes? If the Government cannot guarantee that the total net effect of all the tax changes it will bring about through its so-called tax reform will not mean that ordinary Canadians will pay more in total taxes than they do at present, or for that matter more than they were paying before the last two Budgets, then I say that the Government will be exposed as having as its real purpose, its hidden agenda, another massive tax grab from ordinary Canadians.
Canadians will welcome real tax reform. However, ordinary Canadians are looking for less of a total tax burden, not just some type of Tory shell game in which the peas are moved around from one shell to the other giving an illusion of lower taxes through lower personal tax rates. Instead it will be an over-all heavier tax burden as a result of other types of taxes such as sales taxes. The signal is clearly there in the Minister's statement.
I wish to conclude by saying that, yes, Canadians want to have real tax reform of the kind I mentioned. However, on the
The Address-Mr. Wilson
basis of this Government's track record over the last two years, there is little-in fact nothing-on the basis of which Canadians can have confidence that the Government will provide real tax reform and will help them rather than create another massive tax grab.
I wish to say that the Liberals, the Official Opposition, will be fighting very strongly for individual Canadians to make sure that they have real tax reform in spite of the reality caused by what has happened before by this Government. Instead of a real tax reform there is nothing more in store for ordinary Canadians than one more massive tax grab.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased and delighted that the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) got to his feet. I thought he would be congratulating us on our economic performance. With respect to our economic record, as the Hon. Member knows, the unemployment rate in Windsor is down to 5 per cent. Housing starts are up well over the rate of increase in the national average. I am sure the Hon. Member would wish to support the economic record of the Government of Canada.
The Hon. Member has raised a number of issues, but as has been the case in a number of his interventions, he has his blinkers on. He only sees what he wants to see. He has talked about the tax record of the Government. He has ignored the fact that we have increased the child tax credit, accelerated the payment of the child tax credit and introduced a very innovative low-income refundable sales tax credit which helps those most in need. He has ignored the fact that we will have eliminated income splitting as of next year, we introduced a minimum tax, we removed the financing gimmicks for yachts and motels, we removed the scientific research tax credit, we very much limited the scope of limited partnerships, we reduced the investment tax credit and we eliminated the inventory allowance. All of these measures are designed to create a fairer, more equitable and more balanced tax system. That is the direction we will continue to take in tax reform.
I would ask the Hon. Member to look not only at certain elements of what has happened in the past but at the broad record of tax reform that we initiated immediately after we came into office. We were presented with such a mess which was built up by the previous Government since 1971 that something had to be done and something had to be done fast.

Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that after the Government has been talking about tax reform for two years, it has now been announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that there will be a further period of consultation and that there will be some announcements in the Budget of February or March of next year followed by possible legislation or further consultation. Effectively, therefore, major elements of real tax reform, if it does take place at all, will not be put in place until 1988 or 1989.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
I do not believe that the tax system can be called fair when total tax freedom is given to people with capital gains of up to half a million dollars. I do not believe that the tax system can be called fair when it has increased the taxes payable by ordinary Canadian families by $1,300 just in the course of the first two years of the Conservative Government. I do not believe the tax system can be called fair when it gives enormous tax concessions to pension contributions made by high-income Canadians who have incomes four or five times the income of the average Canadian worker. I do not think the tax system can be called fair when the situation which the Minister himself finally recognized in his speech exists in which some 80,000 profitable Canadian corporations do not pay any taxes at all every year despite having profits that total perhaps $12 billion or $13 billion.
If the Minister wanted to convince Canadians that he was serious about tax reform, he would have come to grips with those problems which have been created by his Government. He would also have come to grips with those problems which were created by a former Minister of Finance and his successors, the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), who started us on this slippery slope of concessions and loopholes for the corporate sector which is forcing us to reconsider the tax system.
I fear that what the Minister is announcing-

I am afraid that what the Minister announced means that he is going to put pennies in the average Canadian's front pocket and take the dollars out of his back pocket, through the sales tax. That is what he intends to do with tax reform, especially with the increased revenue expected under the proposed sales tax system which has now been announced by the Minister. There is no indication, however, that tax remissions will be allowed so as to make this tax a progressive, not a regressive tax for the average Canadian family.

In looking to fairness, the Minister does not appear to have recognized at all that his plans to increase the sales tax will have an enormous impact on ordinary Canadian families. As a consequence, we are talking about a system which will put nickels and dimes back into people's front pockets while taking $1 bills and $5 bills out of their back pockets. These changes in the sales tax are designed to broaden the tax, to impose it on services and to impose it on many essential goods and services which are now tax exempt. It seems to me that that is part of what the Minister announced just now.
While we in this Party can take credit for the fact that the Minister is finally talking about profitable corporations that do not pay taxes, my Party feels that in order to be really serious about this issue, we must have more specifics rather than the vague generalities which have just been put forward. Are ordinary Canadians in favour of reducing personal income taxes? Yes, of course they are. Are ordinary Canadians, on the
other hand, in favour of the reduction in personal income taxes-

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate you and tell you how very pleased I am to see you back in the Chair. I also take this opportunity to assure you and your colleagues who will be acting in your stead that I am prepared to co-operate fully towards ensuring orderly and especially very constructive debates in this House. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, the atmosphere in the House would be more enlightening if we were always debating positive and progressive issues. But such is not the case, certainly not when it comes to the Speech from the Throne.
At first blush, the speech has something for all groups and all sectors, for everybody in fact. However closer scrutiny reveals that it does not offer much to anybody, a seemingly contradictory statement. Quite simply, the first impression we get is that it is full of wishful thinking and promises which are not followed up by concrete programs.
We in Atlantic Canada did expect to hear about constructive regional development measures, we thought the Government would give special consideration to this problem which explains why the Atlantic region is lagging so far behind the rest of Canada. We expected more because we were led to believe there would be a lot more. Mr. Speaker, none other than the Prime Minister himself had this to say in St. John's, Newfoundland:

"The fact of the matter is yes, there has been a substantial economic comeback in Canada over the last two years-but that wealth is not being fairly shared and evenly distributed across the country.
So we have got to re-examine fundamentally some programs and attitudes because Canada is capable of generating tremendous wealth and prosperity.
But opportunities must be fairly and properly distributed and they are not being right now.
October 23, 1986



Mr. Speaker, that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) said in the Atlantic region, but how have those fine words been translated in the Speech from the Throne?
This is what we find in the Throne Speech:
Building on the human and natural resource strengths of the regions, a renewed co-operative effort will lead to a new development agenda.
As a first step in achieving improved results from this sustained national approach, an Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be constituted to facilitate and coordinate all federal development initiatives in the area.
What do all those fine words mean, Mr. Speaker? We now know that they do not mean much, especially after the visit of the Right Hon. Prime Minister to Moncton. Indeed, in his speech the Prime Minister was unable to explain to the New Brunswick Economic Council the role of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency except to say that the Agency would be set up in the near future, by next spring. For the moment, that simply means a reshuffling of bureaucrats and a few changes to bring in an additional level of bureaucracy. I fervently hope that it will not happen.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, businessmen find that there is already much too much bureaucracy. We can also ask the question: Why a new bureaucracy? Certainly not to administer new development programs with new money. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the last two budgets took away hundreds of millions of dollars from the funds allocated to regional development. How can there be regional development if the money required is not there? How can we eliminate regional disparities if the outlying regions are treated exactly the same as the wealthy regions in central Canada?
The Prime Minister was not alone in suggesting that the Speech from the Throne would pay special attention to regional development. Last September, the Atlantic Ministers arrived in Moncton for a conference called "Focus on the Atlantic". They had come to hear the views of the residents and business people of the Atlantic region and to assess the situation. These people gave the Minister the same message as they had given the Prime Minister the week before in Fredericton. I am sure that you recall the visit of the Prime Minister to Fredericton. That was where the workers threw their hard hats before the Prime Minister. Afterwards, the Prime Minister promised the workers that the Atlantic Ministers would listen to the representations of the CN workshop employees in Moncton.
This is what they did. The Ministers took a few minutes to listen to the representations of the workers.
However, Mr. Speaker, while they may have listened, they did not hear anything. On that same day, there was a demonstration bigger than anything people had ever seen in Moncton in front of City Hall. This demonstration was significant because the workers wanted to show their dissatisfaction not only with the way the CN workshops were being dealt with, but also with the attitude of this Government to the problems of the Atlantic.
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
In spite of this demonstration, the Ministers failed to understand the situation. Two weeks later, there came the announcement of a program which is nothing but a joke, and even an insult.
How can we, in the Atlantic region, believe this Government really wants to help the disadvantaged regions?
What is even worse is that we are being compared to the Third World, to countries such as Bangladesh.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall another example of the indifference of this Government, this time in relation with the jobs strategy. Here again, there have been cutbacks. There is much less money in this program than before. What is even stranger is that the changes made to the program favour the regions where the private sector plays a major role in job creation, which is not the case of our own region because our private sector is quite weak.
Let us turn now to fisheries, an industry which is most important for the Atlantic area and especially for my constituency of Westmorland-Kent. If you read that part of the Throne Speech that is written in French, you could believe in this Government's good intentions, Mr. Speaker. Listen carefully.
"La peche est une activite economique d'une importance fondamentale au Canada. Afin d'assurer une plus grande securite a nos pecheurs et de proteger leurs investissements, mon gouvernement accordera une attention particuliere a Tamelioration des ports pour petits bateaux dans toutes les zones de peche." That was all very good. One would believe that they had the best intentions in the world and that they were going to do something. But reading the English text:
To provide increased safety for our fishermen and to protect their material investments, my government will place special emphasis on improving the management of small craft harbours in all fishing areas.

Mr. Speaker, as seen by the people of the Atlantic area, the English text is much more accurate and better reflects this Government's actual intentions.

The intention of this Government is "make believe that you are going to do something".
The lobster fishermen in New Brunswick are worried about the increase in poaching activity. The fishermen would like to see the Department of Fisheries and Oceans put more effort towards the protection of the lobster stocks in particular. The budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has been reduced to such a level that patrol boats worth $200,000 to $300,000 can only afford fuel for two to three days of the week.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
[ Translation]
It's absolutely shocking.

Enforcement officers cannot work extra hours and furthermore, they are tied to their desks because they have no fuel to run their patrol vehicles.

Flow can one believe this Government is sincere! The other primary sectors, like farming and the forest industry, are very briefly mentioned although they are of the utmost importance to the development of our communities.
Let us turn to tourism. As we know, Mr. Speaker, the tourist industry is an important job provider in the Canadian economy, in the Atlantic and throughout the country. Indeed, it accounts for 600,000 jobs in Canada and its growth potential is tremendous. This is an industry that can create the greatest number of jobs in the shortest time frame. In spite of that potential, its growth is only 8 per cent in Canada, as compared with a 13 per cent growth rate on the international level.
It is clear, yes abundantly clear, that the vast number of taxes introduced by this Government since it was elected certainly did not help the tourist industry.
Mr. Speaker, in the last two years I have been listening to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism brag about this Government's concern for the industry. The Government has bragged about having created an independent portfolio for tourism, but what happened to the Department of Tourism in the last Cabinet shuffle? In June last, the Prime Minister simply struck it off. The Department of Tourism is no more. We now have a Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism.
TIAC Chairman, Walter Tilden, expressed his disappointment by saying that it would appear the Government does not know what to do with tourism. The Executive Director of TIAC, John Lawson, also expressed disappointment by saying:
We're back to a combined ministry. That's a clear sign that tourism is once again relegated to a back room.
Just think how disappointed these people must be after reading the Speech from the Throne. Nowhere in the Throne Speech is the word "tourism" mentioned. The Government has forgotten all about tourism.
One of the best years for tourism was 1986. Expo 86 was a prime contributor to this success. We should have taken advantage of the situation to consolidate our position in the international tourism industry. However, the Government has refused to increase its level of marketing abroad. Because of inflation and the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, the marketing budget has been considerably eroded. It is not putting as much money as it should be into that marketing
strategy. The Government just chose to forget the industry. It has broken all the promises made during the 1984 campaign.

What else should I say, Mr. Speaker? I could go on and on. I have not dealt with all the industries, but as seen from Atlantic Canada, the Throne Speech points to more difficult times ahead, because this Government does not seem to care about outlying regions. The more so because this Government did not succeed in gaining public confidence.
What about the answers given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), who will not take a stand and oppose the recommendations that would jeopardize the whole unemployment insurance scheme-the Forget report recommendations. He simply would not take a position. That is very disquieting!
Mr. Speaker, it is to be hoped that the Prime Minister understood the message the fishermen delivered to him when he visited Moncton, for they were anxious to express their dissatisfaction and concern in connection with the Forget report recommendations.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, may I add that I hope this Government will wake up in time, especially to prevent the Atlantic region to suffer a setback vis-a-vis the other Canadian regions. This Government must announce concrete programs and measures to develop primary industries and reduce regional inequalities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to congratulate you on your reappointment to the position of Assistant Speaker.
It is an honour for me to have the opportunity to respond today to the Throne Speech and to talk on a subject relevant to my part of Canada, that of regional industrial expansion. I wish to explain to the House that Atlantic Canadians, the so-called poor cousins of Confederation, are the people best suited to tackle their own problems. Given the chance, we will demonstrate to other Canadians that we are again capable of regaining our place as a world leader. As has often been quoted; "Those who do not know and understand their history are doomed to repeat it". To demonstrate the requirements of the Atlantic provinces better I will use my riding as an example.
South West Nova is the oldest settled part of Canada. Although generally typical of many parts of the Maritimes, it is also very unique. The first permanent European settlement in North America began at Port Royal when a French nobleman, Sieur de Monts, established a "habitation" from which to base his trade in fisheries and furs. He brought with him the first resident geographer, Samuel de Champlain, the First pharmacist, the first surgeon, the first poet, playwright and lawyer, Marc Lescarbot, and a few years later the first European woman to be resident in Canada.
The first highway in Canada was built at Port Royal in 1606 and the first successful agriculture development took place there. The first water-powered mill was erected at this site and the first ships to be built in North America were soon sailing from the Annapolis Basin. The First conversion of a native Canadian to Christianity took place in 1606 when Membertou, Chief of the Micmac Indians, was baptized. The first social club in North America, the Order of Good Time, was founded by Champlain to make the people's stay more enjoyable.
In 1621, King James of Scotland and England granted Nova Scotia, Latin for New Scotland, to Sir William Alexander, and an original manuscript copy of this charter will soon be deposited at the Fort Anne museum.
In 1629, the First Scottish settlement in the new world began at Fair Haven near the site of the French colony. At this time, Nova Scotia was granted its own flag and coat of arms, the first in North America.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Comeau
As time went by, many battles were fought over the ownership of Acadia or Nova Scotia and most took place within the boundaries of my riding.

Over the years, the ownership of Acadia or Nova Scotia led to many fights and, as I said, most of them took place within my own riding. In the end a peaceful climate was restored in Nova Scotia, but not before quite a few Acadians were uprooted from their homes and exiled to Europe, the West Indies and New England.
Mr. Speaker, the best way to show how tenacious those people were is to recall that hundreds and hundreds of them walked thousands of miles through forests and across rivers to find their homeland. As it happens, Mr. Speaker, I am a direct descendant of these remarkable people and living proof of the love-sometimes unfathomable to foreigners-that we the residents of the Maritime Provinces have for our land and our way of life.
Other Canadians simply cannot appreciate this heartfelt sentiment which binds us to our homeland and our heritage and which makes it impossible for us to forsake them. If they cannot understand that, Mr. Speaker, what more can I say?

Immigration into the Maritimes had pretty well ceased by about 1850. The New England planters in the 1760s, the United Empire Loyalists in 1770s and 1780s, the freed slaves from the United States and the displaced farmers and crofters from Scotland, Ireland and England who came afterward had taken up most of the available land by then. This was at a time when half of Canada had hardly seen a settler. It is no wonder that we in Nova Scotia look upon the western provinces as being relative youngsters.
The sea has always been an integral part of the life of the Maritimes. I wonder whether those Canadians who belittle our former prosperity know that in the Maritimes at the time of Confederation we had the fourth largest merchant fleet in the world. It may seem hard to believe, but it is true nevertheless. With a population of perhaps one million people at most, we were competing on an equal footing with Great Britain, France, the United States, Russia, Spain, Germany and Japan. The Town of Yarmouth in my riding had more ships registered than any port in the world, more than London, Portsmouth, Calais, Amsterdam or Boston. Where did this prosperity go, you may ask, Mr. Speaker. When Nova Scotia was dragged into Confederation, kicking and screaming, I should add, the trade policies of central Canada took the prosperity up the St. Lawrence River to Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor and many other such communities. That prosperity has never returned. We have been reduced to the embarrassing dilemma of coming to Ottawa hat in hand looking for assistance.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in his speech the other day, it is not more dollars that we need in Atlantic Canada as much as the ability to make the decisions as to how the dollars that we have will be spent.
Ever since Confederation people in Ottawa have been telling Maritimers what is good for them. But really, Mr. Speaker, they have been looking east with blinkers on. They only see what they want to see. That will not help us regain our prosperity.
The Atlantic provinces must be allowed to run their own affairs and make their own decisions. One hundred and twenty years of simulated indulgence from central Canada has left us relatively worse off than when we started.
I am sure that those remarks will have some of our detractors question our patriotism. The patriotism of the people of Nova Scotia can never be questioned. We have defended our country in her time of need with no hesitation. People of all heritages, Indians, French, English, Irish, Scottish, African, and others, have willingly answered the call. In my riding of South West Nova we have the West Nova Scotia Regiment, successor to the first English regiment in Canada, Phillip's 40th Foot, first raised from among the citizens of the Annapolis Valley in 1717.
I personally know many veterans who fought to keep our country free. If I may digress for a moment, I am extremely pleased with the Department of Veterans Affairs under the capable direction of the present Minister who has vastly improved the direction of programs and their delivery to our many worthy veterans. In the town of Middleton in my riding we have Royal Canadian Legion Branch No. 1. I do not think anyone need question our patriotism in the Annapolis Valley.

Let us get back to the topic of my remarks. We residents of the riding of South West Nova have a diversified way of life. Industries based on the development of resources such as forestry and agriculture are often interconnected with one another or with the fishing industry. It is not exceptional to see a farmer doing some fishing, or a fisherman felling trees to earn a few extra dollars.
Given the kind of land and geography we have, a worker may indeed have two or three different sources of income. In winter, when farming and fishing activities are practically nonexistent, many of my constituents would like to work their woodlands. Current forest development programs-locally administered, I would point out-offer them this kind of opportunity. Perhaps this might serve as an example.

The people of my riding are adaptable and versatile. Our agricultural industry includes everything from dairy production to grain growing to hog ranching and fur farming. Some farmers combine two or three aspects of farming in order to best compete in the market-place. One might say that we do not put all of our eggs in one basket.
The federal Government is also a big employer in my riding. We have several national parks, including the first national
October 23, 1986

historic park in Canada, Fort Anne. We have the Canadian Forces basic training establishment at CFB Cornwallis, and many of my constituents are employed by CFB Greenwood, the air base just outside of my riding. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans provides employment for many others. As well, we have the largest tin mine in North America.

We also contribute substantially to the textile industry and as you can imagine, shipbuilding represents an important area of employment. Our plant used for the manufacturing of ambulances and mobile operating rooms to be sold abroad show that we have the capacity to compete on the international level.
Because of Canada's geography, it is often easier for us to meet competition abroad than in Canada. Year after year Nova Scotia sells Christmas trees in the United States for a total of $30 million. Of course, such an operation only provides part-time jobs for many people, but it is an essential source of additional revenues.

Economists will advise that regional development must be based on comparative advantage. Atlantic Canadians have long known that the emphasis must be on what a region does well. Historically, since the earliest days of European settlement, much of Nova Scotia's economy was based upon shipping and international trade. This led to the development within the province of considerable expertise in serving diverse world markets, and to the establishment of sophisticated transportation networks to facilitate this activity. Those historic skills and patterns have continued to the present day.
Foreign exports of Nova Scotian goods in 1983 were valued at $1.1 billion. The largest item of export from the province is fish products which account for 38 per cent of total exports, valued at approximately $418 million. Nova Scotia is ideally suited to harvest the rich resources of the northwest Atlantic. The province has developed an impressive on-shore fish processing industry. South West Nova alone has 90 of the 160 Nova Scotia fish processing plants. Canada is the world's largest exporter of sea food products, and all indications are that the richness of its fisheries resource will enable it to maintain its position.
In both landed value and weight, Nova Scotia is a leader in Canada, contributing 28 per cent of the total Canadian fishery products export value. Nova Scotia is located adjacent to some of the world's best fishing grounds. It is also situated directly on the major trading route between North America and Europe. Shipping fish products can be done very efficiently. Ferries operate daily between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbour, Maine, and between Digby, Nova Scotia, and Saint John, New Brunswick, carrying refrigerated trailerloads of fresh fish products to markets in Canada and the northeastern U.S. My riding alone accounted for 8.7 per cent of the 1983 landed value of fish for all of Canada. To put this in perspective, my riding alone had more land value than the
The Address-Mr. Comeau
whole Province of Quebec. My riding alone had nearly twice the landed value of the whole province of P.E.I. My riding of South West Nova had approximately the same landed value as the whole Province of New Brunswick.
In 1981, the fishing industry in my riding accounted for 4,560 direct jobs. However, listen to this. A 1985 study undertaken by the Gorsebrook Institute for Atlantic Canada Studies, found that the independent fish processors are misunderstood by both government and economists. The 1983 Kirby Report on the East Coast fishery had done little to explain the operations or to address the problems facing the Nova Scotia independent processing sector and the thousands of fish plant workers who depend on this vital industry. The Kirby Report had focused primarily on the economic problems of Atlantic Canada's giant fish processing firms. Our independent operators survived the difficulties of the early 1980s and were able to maintain the thousands of jobs they provide in rural Nova Scotia. They did this without millions of bail-out dollars from the taxpayer.
The role of the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans is central to the concerns of fish processors in Nova Scotia. Although there is some respect for DFOs efforts to preserve and regulate access to fish stocks, the general tenor of processors' comments is quite critical of government performance, the report says. This dissatisfaction during the summer of 1984 focused on regulatory activity at the individual plant level and on anticipated negative effects of the refinancing of the large Atlantic processors. Small and intermediate size plant owners are convinced that the restructured companies will have to to turn to Government and seek additional support within the next five years.
The success of independently owned fish plants still lies in their ability to react more quickly in their communications and decision-making, and they are more likely to provide the direct supervision necessary to run a profitable company in a labourintensive industry.
The misunderstanding is still there in many parts of the Ottawa decision-making process. This is why the factory freezer trawler decision was greeted with such suspicion and apprehension. The ongoing problems of small craft harbours has preoccupied the fishing industry for many years now and the decision-makers in Ottawa will have to deal with this issue.

No government activity is more important than transportation for the Atlantic Provinces. As it is necessary to ensure that businesses in the Atlantic area overcome the geographic obstacle to compete on national as well as on international markets, the constant presence of the Government in the transportation system is mainly justified. As a result of subsidies and various regulations, the transportation system has become an efficient tool for economic development.
On the whole, the general direction of transportation reform will contribute to increase the efficiency and productivity of

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Comeau
the transportation system. However, this market-oriented approach is giving rise to a deep concern, because we have to determine how communities will be attracted by the setting up of a freight and passenger service.
The importance of transportation for the citizens of South West Nova was clearly shown last year when federal decision makers tried to abolish the wintertime service of the M.V. Blue nose. The people considered such a move as an attack against the basis of their economy.
As pointed out earlier, Atlantic Canada has relied on international trade for almost 400 years. We have learned to compete with the best in the world. Atlantic Canadians have much to gain from successful bilateral trade talks. We recognize that the security of markets must be assured.
Atlantic Canada has felt the effect and the damage of countervail actions which are being advocated by the U.S. protectionists. Security of access to markets offers the stability needed to plan investment and production decisions.
The doom and gloomers who fear that we will lose our national culture by competing with U.S. companies must reassess their views of Canada. Their lack of confidence in Canada's ability to compete is a national disgrace.
The opposition Parties have taken to talking about what they call "new money". They do not seem to understand that printing money and throwing it at problems is not the way to solve these problems. A great deal can be accomplished by spending the money more wisely and by removing the barriers of red tape which simply discourage investors.
The Speech from the Throne announced the creation of an Atlantic agency to co-ordinate regional industrial expansion in Atlantic Canada. I welcome this initiative.
It is my hope that this agency will direct and monitor a new over-all industrial strategy for regional economic growth and that decisions will not be made by Ottawa-based bureaucrats. This agency should seek the participation of the private sector, labour, and both senior levels of Government. Finally, the agency should seek to reduce bureaucratic red tape which restricts growth.
Before concluding let me say that I am sure you have heard about the giant Bay of Fundy tides, the highest in the world. I want to end with a quote from the famous Nova Scotian statesman, Joseph Howe, who said:
Brag about your country, boys. When I'm abroad, I brag about everything that Nova Scotia is, has, or can be, and if they top me at everything else, I can always turn around and stump them when I say "And how high do your tides rise?"
These tides are still rising, Mr. Speaker.

I want first to touch briefly on the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in the House today as part of his contribution to the debate on the Speech from the Throne. We are establishing a variety of levels of service and by so doing we are establishing a variety of levels of class of citizens.
In my constituency there is great concern over the potential to eliminate rural routes. We fought off the elimination of three rural routes last spring and we are keeping a watchful eye on things to make sure they do not try the same thing this fall. There is a fear that some of the rural post offices will be closed, and that fear has been encouraged by Canada Post through its actions.
The hours of operation of some of the rural post offices have been cut back. They are now open from Monday to Friday from eight o'clock in the morning to 2.30 in the afternoon. In the case of the Nolalu Post Office and the Gillies Post Office, which are located approximately 30 miles from the urban centre of Thunder Bay, the individuals who live in that rural area and who commute to Thunder Bay, which is the primary place of employment, have been disenfranchised. In order to reach a job at 8 a.m., they have to leave at 7 a.m. or earlier. To reach a job at 9 a.m., they have to leave at 8 a.m. or earlier. They do not get home until 5 p.m., 6 p.m. or 7 p.m. Therefore, they do not have access to their post office. The post office is closed on Saturday so they do not have that option. The postmasters and postmistresses in these communities went to their bosses and said: "Listen. We believe strongly in service. You talked about not wanting to hurt service. We are prepared to offer flexible hours". In fact, they said they were prepared to open for an hour or so in the evening so that citizens who lived around those post offices, who depend on them for communication, could have access. The answer was: "No. Those are the hours".

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The union said no.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Hon. Member said the union said no. That is not true at all, Mr. Speaker. The individuals involved, with permission of the unions, said quite clearly they would be prepared to provide those services. The Government's answer was, no, because the Government is trying to reduce service, and it is doing it on the backs of the rural residents, in particular.
One of the fears people in the rural area have because of this attitude and because of the decision by Canada Post to restrict the hours of operation, is that Canada Post wants those post offices to fail. It wants to see the level of revenue reduced to the point where anyone can see it is not efficient to keep the post office open. That is the feeling of the people in the rural area of my riding as to what is about to happen to them.
The Minister, I gather, has been receiving mail from citizens. The Canadian Labour Congress, in co-operation with the postal unions, has put advertisements in newspapers and has circulated pamphlets to citizens in postal walks, and the pamphlets are being mailed to a variety of individuals. In order
to assist Members of Parliament, the Minister kindly wrote to us and gave us a suggested way in which we could respond. I would like to quote from that suggested response:
I have noted the comments about providing door-to-door delivery for all urban addresses. As you are no doubt aware, Canada's urban population is growing rapidly, and the cost of providing door-to-door delivery to new addresses is so great that to finance it would require either major increases in postal rates or greater dependence on taxpayers' dollars. The Government and Canada Post find those options unacceptable.
Further along it reads:
I am confident that Canada Post will balance its budget within the next two years-
Clearly, the Government has a fixation about deficit reduction regardless of its impact on service to Canadians. If we follow this strange logic further, we will see the day when the Conservatives will be suggesting we eliminate mail service to those northern remote communities which depend on it for food, dry goods and other products because it costs so much to get it there. Or they will be charged more. We already have a separate fee service to send mail to the United States. Perhaps we will have to pay more to send mail to the North. That is one of the dangers of the route the Government is taking.
Let me now turn to jobs. The Speech from the Throne, quite clearly had a target in it for deficit reduction. What it sadly lacked was a target for an increase in employment or a decrease in the number of unemployed, a concrete projection to which the Government would make a commitment. We all know it is not simple. Jobs cannot be created overnight. A plan must be in place to create them. However, we were not even given an indication that there was a plan in place with some figures attached to it.
There are things we can do to create jobs in Canada and, quite frankly, to create jobs in the community of Thunder Bay and the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan. Some of them are not in disagreement with the Government in either a philosophical or a technical way. The question of replacement of the rolling stock for VIA Rail is one such example, something the Liberals promised when they were in office and something the Conservatives promised during the election campaign. It is something for which the former Minister of Transport indicated his clear support since the last election. There are indications from the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) that he supports the concept as well.
Over the last two years people have been working toward the attainment of the decision to replace the rolling stock. The Government in its widsom, and I compliment it on it, decided that it would go the route of a consortium. It was decided that it would ask Bombardier and UTDC, the Urban Transit Development Corporation which owns Can-Car Rail in Thunder Bay, to put together a joint package for VIA Rail. This was done because the Government clearly wanted to have the cars produced in Canada in order to ensure that the employment opportunities regarding the replacement of those cars would be spread reasonably well throughout the system.

October 23, 1986
We have only two passenger rail car manufacturing facilities in Canada. While my constituents and I would have liked to have the whole package we recognize that there is a need to share these jobs.
The process did not go all that smoothly. Design problems were encountered, which prevented the plan from moving forward as fast as it could in terms of the cost estimates. However, those problems were solved. A solution was reached with respect to getting these two double-decker trains to pass each other without a fear of their colliding at the top. After that was solved there came the question of money.
During last winter and into the spring and summer of this year VIA Rail sat down with the consortium to work out the dollars and cents, as well as the design aspects involved. This summer an agreement was reached. The parties involved met with the newly-appointed Minister of Transport. We all appreciate that he was new to that portfolio and that he needed some time to understand not only the process to date but the process that would occur. Quite frankly, the Minister and his cabinet colleagues will have to determine whether or not the Government is prepared to pay the price which VIA and the consortium came up with.
For the last two weeks in the House my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), and I have raised the matter with the Minister. We are clearly in support of it. I met with over 1,000 workers at Can-Car Rail just one week ago. They asked me to bring back a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in support of the project. I would like to read it into the record for Hon. Members. It states:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,
This letter has been circulated on the shop floor of Can-Car Rail in Thunder Bay. The workers at this plant have been waiting now for many months for confirmation from your government that the contract for the construction of double-decker rail cars to replace VIA Rail's antiquated rolling stock will be awarded, in part, to us.
I am sure you can understand that the release last week of a document showing that VIA is in serious financial trouble has caused us a great deal of concern about our own future. We want to say, Mr. Prime Minister, that we believe our future in this industry is largely dependent upon Can-Car Rail securing this contract.
As Canadians, we believe that a viable national rail transportation system is a fundamental and necessary aspect of nationhood in Canada, and we believe that the upgrading of VIA's equipment, particularly the rolling stock, is necessary to maintain an effective and viable system.
Therefore we are working along with our Member of Parliament, Ian Angus, to ensure that the contract we have been counting on for so long will soon be forthcoming. We ask that you make a public commitment to this effect as soon as posible.
Copies of this letter were delivered to the Prime Minister last week. I took the opportunity of asking the Minister in the House either what decision had been made or when it would be made. His response was that before too many suns and moons have passed he hoped to have an answer for me. Well, about seven suns have passed and perhaps a quarter of a moon. I encourage the Minister of Transport, who is here in the House today, to take the opportunity to ask me a question at the end
The Address-Mr. Angus
of my remarks in which he can indicate that, yes, his cabinet colleagues have agreed and the announcement is forthcoming.
The last area I would like to delve into is with respect to a report commissioned by the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) along with his colleagues in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario. It is a report entitled Western Canadian Low Sulphur Coal, Its Expanded Use in Ontario. When the report was released the Minister of Transport had some very positive things to say about the recommendations which it contained. For example, he said that it could result in significant benefits to the Canadian railways, Great Lakes marine carriers and transfer terminal operations. He said that the increased volume in coal traffic would stimulate rail efficiency which would lead to lower rail costs. He also indicated that any reasonable measure that can be taken to improve the competitiveness of western Canadian coal has his support.
When I finally had the opportunity to read the report I became very excited. I became excited for a number of reasons. The report was undertaken initially to see if one of the answers to our acid rain problem in Ontario, basically, and part of Quebec, was through the use of western Canadian low-sulphur coal. This is why the task force was put together and why a great deal of money and a great deal of time was spent doing research. The answer which the task force came up with was that, yes, it is one of the ways in which we can reduce acid emissions. Over and above that what I find exciting are the benefits which will flow to a large part of Canada as a result of adopting the recommendations in this report. I would like to give Hon. Members some examples in this regard.
If low sulphur western Canadian coal is used instead of installing scrubbers in Ontario Hydro plants and we continue to import at the same high levels-in fact even higher levels- high sulphur American coal, then we can create twice as many jobs in Canada. We will be able to bring in more than twice as much revenue to Canadians, with benefits reaching from British Columbia right through to Ontario and even into Quebec.
I would like to mention some specifics. Over-all, 101,000 person-years of employment would be created over the next 15 years which would bring in total incomes of $1.6 billion. In terms of British Columbia, from where the bulk of the coal will come, 28,000 person-years will be created with $444 million of revenue. In Alberta, 39,000 person-years will be created with revenue of $671 million. In terms of Saskatchewan, where there is a lower figure because of the type of coal there, there will be only 1,000 person-years with $12 million in income. For the Province of Ontario there will be created
14,000	person-years for incomes of $301 million.
I would like to wind up this part of my remarks by saying that it is an area that we have to look at because we in Canada will receive the benefits. We will have more people working. We will have more people paying taxes. Therefore it will be a revenue generator.

October 23, 1986

subsubtopic: RICK HANSEN'S GLOBAL JOURNEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Sunday I met and welcomed our roving, rolling ambassador extraordinaire, Rick Hansen, in Montreal. Shaking his gloved hand, I could sense Rick's strength and the tenacity of purpose that has propelled him over 24,900 miles around our globe. I shared in his enthusiastic determination to raise public sensitivities and awareness to the potential of the disabled. His goal to establish a $ 10-million international trust fund for spinal cord research seems to be closer to reality today than when I visited with him and wished him good luck and farewell in Vancouver just two years ago.
Barriers are continually being challenged and overcome by wheelchair users. Physical access to buildings is improving. However, better psychological access to society through attitudinal change is needed as well. Too many people are still more conscious of the wheelchair than of the person in it.
The next few months of battling the Prairies in winter are going to be rough, but Rick Hansen is tough. Our prayers and thoughts will be with you, Rick, and we look forward to your arrival in Ottawa this weekend.

subtopic: ELECTION OF EAST INDIAN CANADIAN TO BRITISH COLUMBIA LEGISLATURE
ELECTION OF EAST INDIAN CANADIAN TO BRITISH COLUMBIA LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday Mr. Moe Sihota was elected to the B.C. Legislature. Mr. Sihota is, I believe, the first Canadian of Indo-Pakistani origin to be elected to any Legislature in Canada.
The peoples of South Asia have come a long way in Canada since the Komagatu Maru with a shipload of would-be Indian immigrants was turned back from Vancouver Harbour in 1914 by a country with then clearly racist immigration laws. There are now 200,000 Canadians of East Indian origin living in Canada.
Mr. Sihota is a lawyer. Although he is only 31 years old, he has degrees in social work and in law. He was formerly a member of the UBC Board of Governors and ombudsman at UBC. He was formerly the President of the B.C. Young New Democrats. He is currently a member of the Esquimalt Municipal Council, and by yesterday's vote of 13,603 to 10,639 he is a member of the New Democrat caucus in the B.C. Legislature.

Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House a regressive and unacceptable decision which was taken by Air Canada. The airline is slashing direct flight service between Edmonton and Ottawa, thus relegating the City of Edmonton to second-class status. What was once a four-hour direct flight can now be an exhausting and time-consuming seven-hour marathon which stops not only in Toronto but also in, God bless us, Calgary.
Transportation and communication links lead to economic activity, they do not follow it. Thus, Air Canada, by this totally unwarranted act is dealing another body blow to an already struggling Alberta economy.
October 23, 1986

How does Air Canada defend this insensitive and needless decision? It does so by claiming that this will lead to better use of its aircraft. My direct observation is that these flights have nearly always been fully booked. Indeed, at times it is difficult to get on a flight.
By arranging its flights to suit its own convenience rather than placing its customers first, Air Canada is being irresponsible. As for myself, I will now fly Air Canada only as a last, unavoidable resort. I have strongly urged others to boycott the airline until this reprehensible decision has been reversed.

subtopic: NATIONAL COUNCIL ON WELFARE'S REPORT ON POVERTY
NATIONAL COUNCIL ON WELFARE'S REPORT ON POVERTY
speechtext:
The report by the National Council on Welfare has provided further evidence of the growing disparity between the rich and poor in Canada. The report outlined that there were close to 4 million Canadians, or 16 per cent of our population, living in poverty. This is more than in 1980. The results also showed that one child in five is growing up in poverty; that single mothers are five times more likely to be poor than families with two parents; and that 60 per cent of female single-parent families are poor.
The Tories continue to peddle the myth that all is well in the land, and that the economic tide is propping up everyone's boat equally. Brutal statistics tell a tale of two cities, a tale of two Canadas, a tale where food banks are on the rise and the lineups are getting longer. There is nothing more humiliating and degrading to a human being than to stand in line for a daily piece of bread. Regrettably, this is a reality. The sooner the Government recognizes it, the closer we will be to successfully combating poverty across all regions.

subtopic: DYNAMISM OF ENTREPRENEURS IN LOTBINIERE CONSTITUENCY
DYNAMISM OF ENTREPRENEURS IN LOTBINIERE CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:
This being Small Business Week in Canada, Mr. Speaker, I should like to lay special emphasis of the dynamic spirit of our entrepreneurs in the riding of Lotbiniere. Their significant contribution to regional economic development and job creation being essential, their achievements deserve praise.
First and foremost, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that Small Business Week will not go unnoticed in Lotbiniere. For starters, the Bois-Franc Chamber of Commerce will hold a
one-day convention and play host to businessmen. In addition, the regional economic organizations in the riding are taking this opportunity to compile a survey of the activities of our entrepreneurs. Among other things, the territory covered by the Bois-Franc Economic Development Corporation reported an increase of 411 jobs over last year and was instrumental in the establishment of 24 new business concerns. For its part the territory covered by the Lotbiniere MRC added eight new companies to its list and thus created 223 new jobs, not to mention the expansion of existing businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to tell the House about the constructive achievements of small business in Lotbiniere, and I can only encourage their representatives to keep up the good work, and to assure them of my full support.

REMOVAL OF MAILBOXES FROM TORONTO STREETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post has once more earned the wrath of the customers it is supposed to serve. Residents of Parkdale-High Park are furious over the removal of mailboxes from their neighbourhoods. Across Toronto 700 mailboxes have been removed and the increased distance between post-boxes is creating both inconvenience and frustration. This high-handed action on the part of Canada Post is further evidence of the lack of regard the Corporation has for its customers.

October 23, 1986
The Canadian public is entitled to fast, efficient service. What we see are rate increases, service cuts, deficits and excuses. Proposals to cut mail delivery and pick-up services are infuriating Canada Post's customers and time is running out on their patience for footing the bills while getting the boot. I call on Canada Post to return the mailboxes to Parkdale- High Park and get on with the job of serving the Canadian public.

COST OF CONSTRUCTING PRISON IN MANICOUAGAN RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, $41 million-think about it for a minute, Mr. Speaker-is the amount of taxpayers' dollars that are literally being frittered away because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wants to play sugar-daddy to his constituents in Manicouagan.
The Auditor General pointed out yesterday that there was absolutely no need for a protective custody prison in Baie Comeau or, for that matter, anywhere in Quebec. Yet the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) rose yesterday and directly contradicted the Auditor General. Other Ministers of the Crown have attacked the integrity, impartiality, and objectivity of the Auditor General. It is inexcusable that that should be done.
It was also revealed today by the Auditor General that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had a member of his own staff sitting on the construction task force to oversee the construction of the Port-Cartier prison. It is obvious why that individual is there-to further the goals of the Prime Minister to continue to porkbarrel in his own riding and to ensure that contracts are given to his friends.

subtopic: IMPROVEMENT IN MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC FUNDS
IMPROVEMENT IN MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, glancing through the report tabled yesterday by the Auditor General, I was pleased to see that he is aware of the Conservative Government's resolve to reduce public outlays even more.
Although he was careful not to comment on specific political programs or trends, he did say he was particularly pleased to receive the February 1986 note concerning tighter resources management which was sent to all deputy ministers and heads of agencies.
He went on to say that the course steered by the Government with respect to resources management is along the line of his earlier recommendations.
Yesterday Mr. Dye expressed satisfaction with our commitment towards improved accountability and better management.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the Government firmly intends to stabilize the management of public funds, and I am pleased that the Auditor General has publicly acknowledged our initiative. All economic indicators are positive and at last we can see the light at the end of the tunnel.

CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am making this statement today on behalf of the Liberal trade critic. It is what he would like to say to his Leader but cannot: "Please, please, tell me what is going on. On Monday I called for the suspension of free trade talks after the U.S. lumber tariff. That leaves us with a policy for everybody-pro, con, and in the middle-but it also leaves us looking exceedingly foolish".

Mr. Speaker, in his report released earlier this week the Auditor General pointed out his concern for the integrity, fairness, and credibility of our income tax system.
The Government takes these concerns very seriously. During the past two years it has ended tax loopholes such as the scientific research tax credit, hotel and recreational vehicle tax shelters, carve-outs, and income splitting. In addition, the Government is phasing out the investment tax credit and the inventory allowance.
This past July the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a comprehensive tax reform review, upon which he expanded this morning. It is aimed at eliminating corporate tax expenditures and reducing personal income tax rates.
October 23, 1986

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He will be aware of the information we brought to the House a few weeks ago that 64 Canadian companies with profits of over $25 million per annum paid no income tax in 1983. We have new information today that in that year there were only 252 Canadian companies with profits in that range.
Given the evidence that one in four Canadian companies having more than $25 million in profits paid no corporate income tax, can the Minister tell us why he simply announces more consultations on tax reform rather than undertaking to bring in measures in next February's Budget which will ensure that those corporations pay their fair share in taxes?

subsubtopic: NON-PAYMENT OF INCOME TAX BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is anyone in this country who would criticize the Government for consulting about something as large and comprehensive as tax reform. I again draw the attention of the Hon. Member to what I have said to him time and time again, and it has not got through his head, that we have acted. We acted in October, 1984, to change the rules on limited partnerships. We changed the rules on the scientific research tax credits and subsequently eliminated them. In the last Budget we eliminated the inventory allowance and changed the investment tax credit. Those four items are contributing factors to the figures which the Hon. Member
October 23, 1986

has mentioned in the course of his question. We have acted in these areas and we are going to act again in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. Could the Minister of Finance explain why he is not prepared to take measures with respect to companies that are making profits-and there are 80,000 of them-and why he is not prepared to promise there will be some action in his next budget in February, instead of following his party's policy of deferment? Both the Auditor General and Canadian taxpayers agree on the need for immediate tax reform.
