speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Three weeks ago, the Government set forth its broad objectives for future action, and four fundamental factors will form the basis for its action. First, the imperative need to maintain among Canadians the same spirit of reconciliation that has pervaded our Government's relation with the provinces; second, the continuing pursuit of economic renewal, without which no major national projects can be realized; third, expanding Canada's international role which should be a reflection of our development as a nation, and finally, the advent of greater social justice which is both the precondition for, and the logical result of, an enlightened democracy.
As the Minister for External Relations, I am responsible for integrating these objectives in our development assistance policy and our relations with other countries.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I believe that durable national reconciliation cannot be achieved by intergovernmental exchanges alone. It will be achieved by Canadians all over this country, working together to improve the well-being of the community, both here and abroad. And I am convinced, and it is one of my priorities as the Minister responsible for the Canadian International Development Agency, that we could involve even more Canadians in our international activities. This implies, first of all, that we make CIDA better known here in Canada, by expanding our information and public involvement programs and also by making the effort to meet people in their own communities.
Recently, I started on a round of visits across Canada, and I intend to meet as many groups as I can that might be interested in our humanitarian activities.
I recently visited the Province of Saskatchewan where I was delighted to find that the leadership role historically assumed by that province in international development is still a reality. As I progress across Canada I will be comforted to know that even in those regions where difficult economic circumstances, such as agricultural prices in Saskatchewan weigh heavily on the livelihood of our citizens, the traditional generosity of Canadians remains one of the basic virtues.
I was in Toronto at the beginning of this week where I had the pleasure of meeting representatives of the Canadian Filipino community to explain CIDA's important new commitments in favour of the Government of Corazon Aquino.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have a right to know how international development funds are used, and I intend to give them that information in the clearest possible terms. But I also want

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mrs. Landry
to make CIDA better known to Canadians and thus attract new recruits who will share our commitment to development assistance for the Third World. To the question: Have we done eveything we could to recruit the maximum number of Canadians and obtain the maximum amount of resources to help three-quarters of the population of this earth in its fight against poverty? I think the answer must be: No.
Granted, the generosity of Canadians is well known, and our efforts to help the hungry in Africa are a recent example.
Before the General Assembly of the United Nations yesterday, I described the ambitious program developed by Canada for helping Africa. I stated, in no uncertain terms, our desire to see the international community stop talking and start taking action. Nevertheless, I remain convinced, and this will be my second priority at CIDA, that we can recruit more allies for our war against underdevelopment.
It is the only way to come to grips with new emergencies as they occur. Excessive urbanization would be an example.
Among the groups which have not always been given their rightful place I would single out women and young people. The integration of women in all our assistance projects is a matter of social justice in the Third World, just as it is here. In the Third World it happens to be a basic requisite for the development of many societies where women are the unacknowledged or ridiculed driving force behind community progress.
We also seek to establish closer links with another sector of our population which has not always enjoyed full freedom to play an important role, and I am referring to young people. My colleague the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) and I will work together to set up new programs under which young people will find it easier to participate in our endeavours to help Third World countries and to promote the interests of Francophones.
Our commitment to strive for a more egalitarian society in this country stems from the premise that, without adopting a paternalistic and dogmatic approach, we must first show full respect for our basic values among those we want to help. Canada's development effort must continue to be inspired by respect for human rights, so that our assistance may never contribute to perpetuating elsewhere the kind of injustices we do not tolerate here.
As well, Mr. Speaker, we will try to find new ways to cooperate with business. For example, our private sector may indeed have a definite and constructive impact on the private sector in developing countries. Nor should we underestimate the dynamism of the private sector and the significance of its innovative contribution.
As always, non-government organizations play a support role in CIDA, so central that they can hardly be considered as new partners. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, we rank first among donor countries with respect to the NGO participation rate. Our NGOs have been given responsibility for implementing major programs. Just recently, for instance, we asked one
of them to manage the Canadian universal immunization program designed for developing countries of the Commonwealth and those of the French-speaking nations. Our NGOs will also play a leading role in the new aid program for the Philippines which I unveiled in Toronto on Monday.
When it comes to bilateral assistance, we co-operate with the various NGOs even more closely than before. There has been noticeable improvement in this respect since we first came to office.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced, and I am determined to prove, that we can extend even more the contribution of nongovernment organizations and all voluntary associations to our activities. We shall also ask for the participation of organized agencies which have not yet used their abilities to provide assistance to the Third World, such as the municipalities. In other words, we shall explore every avenue of co-operation because Governments alone will never be able to solve the problem of under-development.
We can however hope that concerted action by all sectors of industrialized societies will have a major impact on the tragic situation which still exists in the Third World.
We shall never forget that our major partners in the fight against under-development are those we want to help, and they should be able to become, with our assistance, the artisans of their own economic development.

It is also my belief, Mr. Speaker, that now is the time to take stock of our foreign aid programs. CIDA will be 20 years old soon. The last comprehensive review of development assistance programs was done in 1975. Since then, the world has not been sitting still. On the contrary, it has changed at a quickening pace.
I am convinced that it is high time we take a fresh look at the policies shaping our foreign aid program so we can maximize their efficiency. At the end of the last session the Special Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations tabled its report. The Government will be responding shortly to its recommendations. The Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs will also be submitting an important report on the international financial system and the difficult problems for developing countries concerning debt repayment. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade is presently conducting an extensive study of our foreign aid. I will of course give the fullest consideration to the conclusions of these parliamentary committees. It is also my intention to seek advice beyond the precincts of Parliament and to elicit the largest possible contribution to our reflections from the Canadian public.
This exercise must not be seen as just administrative housecleaning. It is our imperative duty in the light of human suffering to achieve the greatest possible efficiency in delivering aid.

During this Parliamentary session, Mr. Speaker, Canada will have an opportunity unique in its history to enhance its international influence.
Indeed, our country will successively host the Summit of francophone countries, the Summit of the Commonwealth and the Summit of industrialized countries.
If I may, I would like to speak further about the Francophone Summit where I had the honour of representing Canada with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in my capacity as Minister for External Relations.
I am indeed especially proud to remind this House that, had it not been for the historic vision and enlightened policies of our Prime Minister, this Summit would perhaps never have taken place.
As far as I am concerned, this is one of the best results of our initiatives to promote national reconciliation. Could anyone have imagined a few years ago that the Canadian and Quebec Governments would be able to organize jointly on our territory a meeting of the countries that have French as a common language, and that the First Ministers of Canada, Quebec and New Brunswick would agree on a harmonious Canadian participation in this new international forum?
The major role played by Canada at the first Francophone Summit last February in Paris is also the result of a judicious definition of our potential participation and of our expectations from this francophone forum. First of all, we want these meetings to provide an opportunity to exchange practical and profitable projects. For us, the Summit is not a dream come true. It is already a meeting of collaborators. We shall bring to it our share of precious knowledge and we expect to gain in return an enriching experience.

It is a happy coincidence that the meeting of the Commonwealth heads of state and government will also take place in Canada during the life of this Parliament. By hosting both the Francophone and Commonwealth Summits, Canada implicitly says something about the very special role it can play in today's world and tomorrow's. We are the only industrialized country that belongs to both of these important groups. Our recent strides toward national reconciliation are helping us to play a vigorous role in la Francophonie, and within the venerable Commonwealth we have recently shown new leadership, notably in the urgent matter of South Africa.
Canada's history owes a lot to France and England. How fitting it is that it is now recognized in the French-speaking and English-speaking countries of the world as a unique bridge between these two large families of nations.

As you see, Mr. Speaker, the coming year will be a great year for Canada on the international scene. I for one am very pleased that Canadians will have an opportunity, because of the three summits that will be held here, the Francophonie, the
The Address-Mrs. Landry
Commonwealth and the Industrialized Nations, to measure the full extent of this country's role within the world community.
I also welcome the coming opportunity to play host to our African friends, whether through the Francophonie or the Commonwealth meetings. As I said once again before the United Nations yesterday, our Government, after having responded positively to the critical situation in Africa last year, has no intention of reducing its help to that continent now that other subjects are making the headlines.
I have already said, Mr. Speaker, that I also want this new parliamentary session to give us an opportunity to refine our strategy for development assistance. So, to conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me assure this House that I will make every effort to develop the most effective assistance program possible and to conduct external relations that bring tangible results.
Canada's prestige is at stake, but more important still, millions of human beings in need are looking forward to it.

Again having a special interest in that area, I am pleased to see that the Africa 2000 program is well under way. Of course, the third area is the focus on women and development. As I have had the opportunity of either travelling to some of the countries with which we are involved, or during the summer welcoming representatives from those countries at Expo, I have heard over and over again just how important that is. It is women in so many of the lesser-developed countries who are bearing the burden of poverty. If they are going to make advances in their economy, it is going to be so often the women who are going to do it. Whatever we can do to strengthen their role in these countries is vitally important.
With respect to Africa 2000, I still find that across the country there is a lack of understanding about what we are trying to do in Africa. I think it is important that there be some component of that program directed toward public education. I wonder if the Minister might comment on that and advise the House if there would be programs in this respect.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mrs. Landry
As to the Filipino assistance program, can she advise the House how Filipino-Canadians can become involved in the new program and what might be the appropriate kinds of assistance they could provide and what the next steps are going to be in the development and delivery of the new assistance program for the Philippines?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely thank the Hon. Member for her concern for the cause of development and also for her reference to the announcement I was pleased to make Monday in Toronto concerning the Philippines, for her concern for the Philippines community. I feel the Government's commitment was a gesture of support to Mrs. Aquino's new government, which has shown a positive commitment to her country's social and economic recovery. So the announcement we made was aimed at supporting Mrs. Aquino's policy.
The Canadian Philippine community was very pleased with our announcement. I told them that of course the program orientation was decided upon after a planning mission was sent to the Philippines in September, with a delegation made up of CIDA officials and representatives from the Philippine-Canadian community who met the Government, the NGO's and everyone concerned with the development of the Philippines. These people came back with certain priorities with which we will try to deal as quickly as possible.
We are conscious that at present the Philippines need some short-term assistance and we are therefore considering shortterm and eventually long-term programs. We rely greatly of course on the support and contribution of Canadian groups of Philippine origin. We told them that we will keep in contact with them, that they can apply to the organization, to CIDA and that we would be pleased to develop jointly with them, and of course with the Philippine authorities programs, which will meet our commitments to the Philippines.
Therefore, I am quite pleased to indicate to this House today that we greatly rely on the contribution of the Canadian community of Philippine origin.
My dear colleague's second concern was related, I believe, to the Africa 2000 program. Africa 2000 is a program which we announced last spring and which was an additional commitment of our Government to Africa. This was a $ 150-million commitment for a 5-year period and we have asked more specifically for the assistance of the NGO's. A slice of $75 million has been allocated to the non-governmental organizations which are to develop and submit to us programs designed in keeping with our commitments to the needs of Africa.
Also, there is a whole development assistance program to foster women's integration.
My hon. colleague has also indicated her interests in the community of women; I am pleased therefore to repeat that within the framework of the Africa 2000 program, we have allocated an envelope of $25 million for the integration of
women in the development. I should like to mention some of the commitments: $10 million to finance health-related projects; $2 million for the assistance program with the United Nations; $6 million for studies aimed at promoting university education among women. I think, therefore, that the Canadian Government has committed itself not only in words, but also in deeds by taking steps to favour the integration of women in the development.
Of course, you mentioned also how the program is and should be promoted throughout Canada. As I indicated a while ago, I am anxious, during my travelling from coast to coast, to inform the public about the Canadian International Development Agency. I refer to the various projects in which Canadians can participate, and I hope, through this initiative, to recruit new partners to help us develop our projects for Africa, in order to meet even more efficiently the urgent needs of Africans.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to take part in this debate on the Speech from the Throne. Not long ago, on the afternoon of October 1, 1986, several experts used the expression "deja-vu" to describe the last Throne Speech. Personally, I feel that the term "rehashed" fits better. Why? Because the Prime Minister had delayed by as much as a whole month the opening of the session to give his new Ministers the time to make their contributions to the Throne Speech. Yet, we have been hearing the same platitudes as in November 1984, at the opening of the first session, when we heard the promises made during the election campaign of the preceding summer. Today, Mr. Speaker, we can rightfully conclude that the more it changes, the more it is the same.
Mr. Speaker, we find in this nice little booklet, the Speech from the Throne opening the second session of the 33rd Parliament, an item which is not altogether new. One should not forget the Blue Paper of November 5, 1984, dealing with a new direction for economic recovery. The time has come for us to assess this economic recovery the Government keeps harping about in its Throne Speeches. In assessing those results, I would like to quote an article by Alain Dubuc in the September 6, 1986 issue of La Presse. This is what he says appropriately of those two years of Conservative administration:
The same thing all over again. Economic growth: it is the best way of determining if the growth of the economy is adequate. Our economy grew by 3.3 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984, the last two years of the Liberal administration. In 1985, the growth rate slowed down to 4.5 per cent and should not exceed 3 per cent this year, as we are entering a slowdown phase. There has been no progress on that account.
This is Mr. Alain Dubuc, from La Presse, not me, speaking. And it is quite clear. In this economic renewal process, our

October 23, 1986

economic growth is not going forward, but backward. Obviously, there is no progress.
But there is more, Mr. Speaker. In the same assessment, in that article of September 6, 1986, Mr. Dubuc writes, and I quote:
Inflation: Price increases had already been slowed down to 4 per cent in the Summer of 1984 when the Liberals were defeated. And no progress has been recorded since. Dollar: Our currency was worth 77.14 US cents in August 1984. It is now worth only 72 cents, after falling below 70 cents in last February.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you will correct me if I am wrong, but I think that presently it is below 72 cents, around 7116 cents.
Purchasing power: This is the measure of consumer prosperity. However, in 1985, while inflation increased by 4 per cent, salaries increased only by 3.5 per cent. The same trend seems to be prevailing this year. And while the purchasing power will therefore have decreased by 1 per cent, the tax burden imposed by the Federal Government will have increased by 23 per cent.
That is what the Conservative Government means by economic renewal, Mr. Speaker. Reducing the purchasing power of consumers.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has been boasting about massive investments since they took power. Let us see what Mr. Alain Dubuc says, and I quote:
Investments: Renewed confidence in businesses was going to be the key to the Conservative success. This excitement is usually reflected in the investments of the private sector.
Now they will increase by a mere 2.8 per cent this year, that is at a slower pace than the economy generally.
In the export field, Mr. Speaker, we know quite well that for several months our governments have been discussing free trade with the United States. And let me quote again from that report:
Exports: This other source of vitality for the Canadian economy, or foreign trade has also decreased. In 1984, our Canadian exports exceeded our imports by $20 billion. This year, that excess will be reduced to around $12 billion. As a result the balance of payment surplus which amounted to $2.5 billion two years ago could turn into a record deficit of $8 to $9 billion this year.
And finally, Mr. Speaker, the other very important factor of economic renewal in which the Conservative Government takes pride and for which it takes credit is job creation. Of course we have been told so many times in this House about the 500,000 jobs that have been created. That is the fact, and Mr. Dubuc indeed is not overlooking it. I quote him:
Job creation-This is where the Mulroney Government put its pride. From August 1984 to August 1986, 569 000 jobs have been created in Canada. However the figures seem to indicate this was done in one shot. Since the beginning of 1986, not one job has been created in Canada. There were 11,632,000 jobs in January; there are now 11,615,000, or 17,000 less than at the beginning of the year.
Mr. Speaker, that is the score, and I would like to add this to what Mr. Alain Dubuc stated on the matter of job creation, concerning the 569,000 jobs. Mr. Speaker-how could the Conservative Government create those 569,000 jobs? Mr. Speaker, the truth should be stated once and for all. How could they? We are all aware that before the Conservatives came to power, we Liberals had an employment program called Works Canada. It was a 52-week employment program. As a matter of course the Conservative Government abolished
The Address-Mrs. Landry
that program and created 26-week job creation programs. This means the same programs that used to create one job now created two. There are the figures. That is how they play with statistics, Mr. Speaker.
But in the end, after a year and a half, we see those programs no longer have the rollover needed, there are no new jobs created anymore. On the contrary, we have lost 17,000 during the first six months of 1986. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker.
And once again, on October 1st they come up with a speech on economic renewal. Mr. Speaker, I would not like to miss this opportunity, since this is Small Business Week in Canada. Last summer, I had the pleasure of travelling across the land, from Vancouver to Halifax, and meeting with people, businessmen and women who were concerned about small business development in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, during all that time, during those meetings, I was leading that Liberal task force on small businesses. People submitted that the time had come for the Government of whatever stripe, red, blue or green to stop the rhetoric on small business, to stop putting people to sleep with the suggestion that small business is the most wonderful thing in the world, and to start helping those who really need it.
I should like to tell Hon. Members how a Cornwall businessman defined small business when he appeared before our task force. I should like to quote him, if I may. This will take a few minutes, but I suggest we ought to reflect upon this definition of what is a real Canadian entrepreneur.
Today's small businessman is faced with overwhelming odds. He is faced with "Big Government" who legislate laws that govern every decision he makes and every action he takes. He has to know about labour laws, corporate laws, workmen's compensation laws, tax laws and I could go on and on. He is swamped by paper work, in order to satisfy the whims of every bureaucrat who administers and enforces these laws.
He also has to run his business, buy the products, wheel and deal prices, sell his product or service at a profit, meet ever increasing competition from larger big businesses, satisfy his bank manager, work long hours and all too often with very little left for himself. He is the head office, the bookkeeper, the buyer, the salesman. He is also on the front line, accessible to all, not only customers, but also the target of every charitable organization, sports club or service club who wish a sponsorship or a donation. Yet, you will find him coaching a minor hockey team, leading a charity drive, attending a service club or merchants' meeting and serving on a church or civic committee.
This is our average Canadian businessman or businesswoman and what are we doing for them today?

Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne contains one paragraph about small business, just one, and I want to quote it so everybody will remember it:
My Ministers will introduce programs to promote small business and entrepreneurial values. Included will be measures to improve procurement procedures, to strengthen the unsolicited proposals program for small companies and entrepreneurs, to increase technology tranfer from government laboratories, and to develop new initiatives to promote entrepreneurship among youth.

October 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Elere we go again, Mr. Speaker, words, more words, nothing but words! What a beautiful speech! But the Progressive Conservatives have been in office for two years now, so when are they going to start practicing what they preach? Hopefully they will not tell me that the capital gains tax exemption was meant for small business. It is not quite true, and statistics will bear me out, Mr. Speaker. It is happening in major cities, nothing but real estate speculation. If you are on the market for a house, the price has almost doubled. Why? Because of the capital tax exemption. How many jobs has this created? How many times did we point this out in the House?
Now, they are bragging about another pension reform involving the investment of pension funds in small business. Yet, at the same time, they announce that businessmen cannot invest their pension fund in their own business. Mr. Speaker, where is the logic in that? I have just given a definition of what is a small businessman in Canada. How could a municipal pension fund, administered by a board of directors, be invested in a convenience store when no control structure has been provided? That fund is the businessman. When he is gone, there is no business.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if he were allowed to use his pension fund, he could lower his bank loan, pay less interest and therefore expand and enlarge his business which would be less encumbered. But no. That request was made to the Minister of Finance on a number of times. He refuses because he fears that someone might take advantage of the situation and starts playing around. But how? He fears small business which creates the majority of jobs, and this was acknowledged yesterday in the Auditor General's report-actually it was just a press release Mr. Speaker, where it said: 'A tax credit of 225 millions dollars granted by Revenue Canada'. This means, Mr. Speaker, that through the Income Tax Act, tax credits are made legal. And they worry about the fact that small businessmen might invest their pension fund in their own business to create jobs. They refuse, they do not trust these businessmen; who knows they might try to play around with their income tax. It is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. It indicates that the Government does not trust Canadian men and women who are working an average of 16 or 18 hours a day on their business to earn a living, while paying out to large corporations millions of dollars in subsidies. Those are the facts. That is the economic recovery the Progressive Conservative Party has been talking about.
When I travelled this past summer with the Liberal task force on small businesses throughout Canada, I received a great many recommendations. I can assure the House that by the end of November, we will have prepared a preliminary report on this issue, contrary to this Government. We should remember that, Mr. Speaker. In January or February 1985, or in the spring of 1985, the previous Minister of State for Small Businesses announced a consultation from coast to coast. He travelled everywhere in this country to learn, because nowadays, we must pay our Ministers for them to learn. A Minister
must be well educated and well prepared to administer his Department and suggest policies and programs to help the constituency of his Department. But for the past two years, Ministers have been learning. They have been learning every day. They set up commissions and task forces. As I was saying, he was travelling from coast to coast with an army of his officials, paid with taxpayers money, to find out what was the problem with small businesses and what would be the solution before suggesting policies. This is October, 1986. We have not yet received a report, preliminary, final or otherwise, on this ministerial task force, Mr. Speaker.
As for us, we did it without any budget nor public servant. We toured the country on our own money, and in late November we will publish a report and will put forward to Canadians some policies for small businesses.
That's the difference, Mr. Speaker, between the Conservatives and the Liberals. The Conservatives, after 20 years in opposition, came to power without any program, without any knowledge, without any vision, nothing, Mr. Speaker. And today Canadians are suffering the consequences. Some wonder why Canadians have lost confidence in this Government; the answer is very simple, Mr. Speaker. This Governement has no vision. It does not know where to go, as was evidenced today by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). For two years now he has been changing his mind with the weather, considering a value added tax, or a transfer tax, or a tax reform, or increasing personal income tax and reducing corporate tax. Today he is proposing to increase corporate tax and reduce personal income tax. Now, Mr. Speaker, when will that nonsense stop? How much must Canadians pay for that nonsense from this Conservative Governement?
You are indicating that my time is up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this oppportunity to speak today. Many Members will recognize that although the election is some two years past, when we were chosen to lead the country toward the changes it needs, Ministers of the Crown have few occasions to express themselves in debate in the House. I found myself in that position as Minister of State for Mines, so it is with a great deal of pleasure and anticipation that I share a few thoughts with Hon. Members today.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my congratulations and sincere best wishes to you and your elected and appointed colleagues who together serve the House of Commons. Our election process at the beginning of this second session of Canada's Thirty-third Parliament was, for all who participated awkward and arduous, but in its final result a most democratically successful and satisfying exercise of Member power. Let us all hope that Member power, that admirable, even essential, goal of the parliamentary reform process, initiated by the Government, will be reinforced by our future actions and decisions together.

I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) and the Hon. Member for Restigouche (Mr. Girard) for their exemplary contribution at the onset of this Throne Speech debate. They grasped and stressed the positive and constructive elements of our Progressive Conservative government's political program. Their example and the quality of their speeches did serve well those who followed. But finally it was the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, who once again reminded us that our mission, our main mandate, is to introduce and maintain a responsible and stable system of government in order to ensure confidence in ourselves and in the future of our great country.
Areas of progress up till now are not difficult to enumerate and record. It has been done by many others. But that is not enough. We have to show our intentions to follow through, to reduce crippling deficits and ensuing interest rates in order to secure investments and jobs. You can rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that we are committed to keep the promises we made.
The Address-Mr. Layton

I am particularly proud to participate in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne debate because it gives me an opportunity to share some thoughts and, perhaps, feelings about my riding of Lachine with its key role in the historic and economic development of Canada, and its key role today in the economic renewal of the Montreal region. The federal riding of Lachine, which I am proud to represent, is comprised of the four cities which developed along Lac Saint-Louis to the southwest of Montreal. These cities are Beacons-field, Pointe-Claire, Dorval and the southwest section of Lachine. Not known to many, other than the 57 families who, along with my own, live there for six to seven months of the year, Lachine riding also includes the car-free and carefree municipality of the Island of Dorval.

Historically, Lachine was established as a relay post for the celebrated voyageurs, a trading station where those travelling in canoes and those travelling in larger boats could barter wares for pelts and furs. Lachine is where I believe our trade originated without all the intricacies of today. In spite of the changes in means of transportation, communications and technology since the 17th century, the riding of Lachine, with its highways, its railways and its Dorval Airport, still remains the relay point between the economic centre of Montreal and the rest of Canada.

Thus I would like to address very briefly some of the concerns raised by the electors in my riding of Lachine. My neighbours in these lakeshore communities voted overwhelmingly for change in September of 1984. They shared, with a majority of Canadians, the concern that continuing down the road of unlimited government spending would lead to higher inflation and debts that could never be sustained let alone repaid. I believe they support the direction that our Government has taken, but are disappointed that progress is slow and at times intermittent. It would be their wish that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would, in nautical terms, "stay the course" so that a stable, fair and promising future would be the inheritance of all Canadians.
Paralleling this concern for fiscal responsibility and responsible management in Government, there is a frequently raised concern for equity and simplicity in the tax system. My constituents will welcome tax reform as it was announced in this House this morning by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) with its encouragement for and protection of personal savings. Many have expressed disappointment with current regulations that tax and restrict the use of savings and compromise those who accept early retirement packages leaving their long-held jobs open to younger workers.
The business leaders of my constituency warmly support the steps taken by the Government to encourage initiative and

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Layton
reward success. However, they are looking for equal opportunity and uncomplicated access to government Supply and Services contracts and to internationally competitive regulations on research investments and trade activities. They ask simply for the level playing field, that often obscured goal of our trade negotiations, and of course for a chance to get into the game.
My community has been home to many for most of their lives. Families have been raised, schools and churches have been built. Most of my neighbours are looking to the Government to maintain conditions that permit them to continue to live where they are. In recent years, heavy industries located in the east end of the Lachine riding have been particularly affected by the international economic slowdown and recession. Many large companies have either closed down or cut back their operations with the result that jobs and job opportunities have been greatly reduced. One group which has been particularly hard hit by these changes is that consisting of managers and executives over the age of 45 who have, in many cases, been released after many years of service and are unable to find other employment. However, with the enlightened leadership that has characterized the public administration of our municipalities over the years, other interests including the modern technologies of biochemistry, electronics and aerospace have been encouraged to establish and develop operations in our area with its access to transportation, to highly trained human resources and to excellent living conditions. These are the key factors in executive decisions.
Lake St. Louis is a lovely natural playground. However, the absence until recently of industrial and municipal waste treatment systems has cast a cloud of uncertainty on its use for bathing and other aquatic sports like water-skiing and windsurfing. Now, with the combined efforts of all concerned- and I am glad the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is with us today-and with the putting in operation of the vast Montreal urban community sewage collection system, it is hoped and expected that this beautiful waterfront with parks and beaches will be accessible and totally safe to one and all. A population of close to two million Canadians will be able to enjoy it. I believe that all Governments share in the responsibility to develop and preserve these precious natural resources.

And more generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, city residents in my riding belong to the Montreal urban community. We are deeply worried about what is happening in Montreal. For many various reasons, our region did not share in the economic renewal experienced by other areas in 1984 and 1985. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, particularly in the eastern part of the region, but confronted to that problem, the Prime Minister established ten months ago a ministerial committee of which I was a member, under the leadership of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). Its terms of reference were to study the situation and bring forward long-term solutions to ensure Montreal its rightful place in the future.
To help us, our ministerial committee asked a few Montrealers, among the leaders or most informed or experienced people in various fields, to form an advisory committee.
After studying the preliminary report, and a few months ago, the orientation report, the ministerial committee is now preparing specific and practical recommendations to be implemented by the government. Some have already been announced, including the establishment in Montreal of an international banking centre and a high technology centre for aviation and aerospace industry, bio-technology, telecommunications, transportation and engineering services.
I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that if those great orientation projects are pursued Montreal will rank among the firsts as an economic and cultural activity centre. In fact, high technology that is tied to the CF-18 maintenance contract is a very important part of those projects and I hope all ministers responsible for the final decision in that matter will keep it in mind.

Our concerns for the future of Montreal as an economic force in Quebec and as a cultural development centre for Canada find expression also in the arguments being advanced to resolve the problem of the two airports in Montreal. When forecasts of passenger and air-freight traffic indicated in the 1960s that the traffic would soon surpass the ultimate capacity of Montreal's airport at Dorval, the Government of the day decided on a site considerably removed from the centre of the city. Alternative sites near Drummondville to better serve central and eastern Quebec and near Vaudreuil to better serve Ottawa, eastern Ontario and the northern United States were set aside, according to reports, because the chosen site at Mirabel had a lower incidence of fog. Fog was what surrounded and continues to surround the Grits.
Be that as it may, the markets never developed and the hundreds of millions of dollars invested in land acquisition, buildings and infrastructure at Mirabel have never been fully utilized. Having inherited this problem after years of inaction, the Government undertook to resolve the issue first with the farmers whose land had been unnecessarily expropriated. This past year, the Government has completed extensive studies on the best way to serve the air travel market in the Montreal region.
Convenience, cost, access, time and interconnection opportunities are all factors considered by the travelling public. Tens of thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars in new investments will be directly affected by the decision on the Montreal airports when it is taken.
The Government has received opinions from the airlines, the business community and the provincial and municipal administrations directly and indirectly affected. I am confident that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and all responsible will adopt a solution that best responds to these interests and that Dorval airport in the riding of Lachine will continue
October 23, 1986

its 300-year-old role as the gateway from Montreal to North America.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude with a brief comment on the Constitution and the negotiations between the federal government, the signatory provinces and the nice province of Quebec.
At the outset, I would like to state that most Quebecers are first and foremost Canadians, that we are proud to be Canadians and ready to play our part and accept our share of responsibilities as citizens of this great and beautiful land.
Canada without the province of Quebec is unthinkable! It is obvious that the signing of an agreement with the Quebec government must be an important and urgent priority of our government. I hope as well that our concerted efforts will bring about a fair and lasting success.
One particularly delicate element of the constitutional negotiations will be the freedom of all Canadians to live and work together in both of Canada's official languages. Great progress has been made in developing linguistic skills among Canadians, particularly those attending schools in the last 10 or 15 years. Job opportunities in our governments, institutions and business concerns should be equalized as must access to government services and information in either language. I hope that during negotiations the necessary assurances will be found to allow the natural goodwill of Canadians to be applied to the language issues everywhere in Canada. Canada deserves our best effort. Let us be sure we give it.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member. Since the election of his Government in 1984 we have seen the closing up or the sharp reduction in activities of a number of companies which operated in basic industries in the east end of Montreal. I am not saying that they closed up or cut back because of the Government, but this is in fact what happened.
For many years, for generations, the Canadian National Railway operated shops in the City of Moncton, in his City of Montreal and in my City of Winnipeg. Now the CNR has already made arrangements to close the shops in Moncton, turning over the facilities to Canadian General Electric. About 700 workers who have worked for years at the Moncton shops will be out of work. The CNR has announced that it proposes to close up its railway shops in Montreal. If they continue to operate, they will simply operate by way of contract work for other companies.
We heard a message from the Hon. Member about the great things that the present Government is doing for Montreal and Quebec. What advice would the Hon. Member give to those
The Address-Mr. Layton
workers who have worked for so many years in the Point St. Charles shops of the CNR and who are facing unemployment in the very near future?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am happy to have the comment and also the question from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). It is true that Winnipeg, Montreal, and Moncton were the principal centres where the railways chose to build their original service and fabrication centres. It is also true that the railway systems of those days have gone through great changes, not only in the service that they render but also in the equipment that they use to render that service. There has been considerable effort made to rationalize the cost of maintaining our railroad systems. Without it, the railroads would not have the capacity to compete with the other modes of transport. Highway trucking services are very flexible. There is a great deal of competition in rates and service in the market. I am a believer that the railways are a basic form of transport for Canadians and our goods. VIA Rail, CN, and CP organizations are going through a process to create and maintain that degree and quality of maintenance in their centres, and to compete not only nationally but also internationally, as so much of our transport now travels back and forth across the border. The Montreal community had been selected as one of the major service centres on our short term service type role for the VIA operations. Many of these decisions are under review.
As a Montrealer, but more particularly as the Member for Lachine, which is a west end component of that great Montreal region, let me say that we have suffered from the loss of heavy industry jobs at Dominion Bridge, Dominion Engineering and Allis-Chalmers. These jobs are the ones being replaced by a capacity which uses a lot more of our trained minds.
During the last weeks of summer, I had the privilege of visiting a number of very advanced technological centres in the west end of Montreal. I also share with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr.Cadieux) a great interest in the biotechnologies. This has become one of the major future industries for Canada, and certainly for the region of Montreal. We look forward to this continuing to be an opportunity for those trained minds that we all know the country will depend on to find an outlet for their skills.

speechtext:
I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lachine (Mr. Layton) on what was his maiden speech. During that speech he stressed the great necessity for everyone and every province to function in both of Canada's official languages. I would like to commend the Hon. Member further for his enviable command of both of Canada's official languages.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne which we are considering today represents the Speech from the Throne at mid-term of the Conservative Government. It has been in office for two years. Of course the Throne Speech reveals a certain amount of tiredness. It seems that the Government has run out of steam. It is in drift right now.
Canadians hoped to see concrete measures for action, especially in the area of job creation. They were hoping to see some very specific measures for tax reform, equality for women, cultural policy, and environmental protection, all of which are very important public policy questions. However, we only see pretty vague statements. As I said, there is drift. There is no vision in the Speech from the Throne.
There are high-sounding phrases. There is talk about national reconciliation, economic renewal, and social justice. Who could disagree with these as objectives? However, there is precious little to achieve any of them. There is talk about families, and the importance of the family is recognized in the words. However, this is the Government which cut the family allowance and is cutting the child tax credit. How can we believe that it has the interest of Canadian families at heart?
I note that action was promised for victims of child sexual abuse, child prostitution, and violent pornography against women and children. It is about time. These issues have become far worse in recent years. There were unanimous recommendations on child prostitution as long ago as 1983 by the justice committee. The Badgley Commission made extensive recommendations in the area of child sexual abuse, including child prostitution and child pornography. These recommendations have been available since the summer of 1984, and we have not had action on them.
The Throne Speech mentioned a campaign against illicit drugs, but it failed to mention that the great killer drugs are alcohol, which kills 12,000 Canadians per year, and tobacco, which kills 35,000 Canadians per year. These are the licit drugs, and they create a far worse problem in terms of health, damage, loss, and destruction of families. They are not glamorous enough for the Government. It would rather follow
October 23, 1986

Ronald Reagan and go after the illicit drugs which certainly pose problems. There is no doubt about that, but they are not remotely on the scale of the illness, death, and harm caused by other drugs. The Government's priorities are wrong. It is going after issues which it thinks will give it some credibility with the public, but they are not the issues that really count.
The Government talks about economic renewal, but there is very little about job creation in the Speech from the Throne. There is a vague statement about investor and consumer confidence. The Government hopes that somehow this will mysteriously develop and be the solution to the problem of continuing high structural unemployment. Youth was scarcely mentioned although the unemployment rate among young people is even higher than the rate among older Canadians. The educational opportunities of young people have been cut back by the Government in its cuts to Established Programs Financing for post-secondary universities and colleges. These were cut last spring, yet the Government makes vague promises to youth.
I note the promise of the establishment of a new agency to promote economic opportunity in Atlantic Canada. Certainly job creation is needed in Atlantic Canada, but I question the establishment of a new agency. We already have a government Department, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. Will we now have two? Will they send memos to each other? Will the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion get out of job development in Atlantic Canada? Certainly these questions are not addressed in the Speech from the Throne. One reason the Government is not very specific about job creation is that it does not have a good idea. It is very misguided on the subject.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had a prison plan for an area where it was not needed. He moved it into his riding where it certainly is not needed, at an expense of more than $60 million. He justifies it on the grounds of job creation. If he wanted job creation, he should have considered that misguided project against other possible ones which would do a better job at creating good productive employment, long-term jobs. We simply do not see that in the Speech from the Throne. Instead we see very opportunistic schemes being used for political purposes which do not serve the public very well in terms of getting the unemployed back to work.
I was pleased to see the down playing of free trade in the Speech from the Throne. In fact the Government sounds almost like the NDP in how it is now treating free trade. It talks about trade with all parts of the world. It especially mentioned the Pacific Rim, an area in which we can certainly expect to expand our trade. It talks about mutually advantageous trade with the United States instead of a free trade agreement which would probably lose us a lot of jobs and certainly risk our political and cultural sovereignty. Whether the Government has stepped backward for the right motives or the wrong ones, whether it has just been reading the poles, or whether it has been convinced that the interests of Canadians will not be well served, I do not know. However I am pleased
The Address-Ms. McDonald
to see this more cautious approach to free trade. It was never a panacea for our economic ills. I am glad to see it not being touted quite as enthusiastically in the Speech from the Throne as it was in the past.

Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne refers to national reconciliation, social justice and economic renewal. Yet, nothing impressive is planned to meet these objectives, however worthy they may be. There is even a step back in the Government policy on national reconciliation. The previous Speech from the Throne was stronger in this regard. The latest Throne Speech recognizes that the Charter of Rights and Freedom and the Canadian Constitution remain incomplete without the assent of Quebec. That is the least that can be said. What the Government undertakes is vague and weak, and I quote:
Should there appear reasonable prospects for agreement, formal negotiations will proceed in the expectation that Quebec will take its rightful place as a full partner in the Canadian Constitution.
That is very little. We have to wait for reasonable prospects, but where will they come from? We should instead be creating prospects for an agreement.
In relation with social justice, the Government talks about building a modern, tolerant and caring nation in which its citizens are secure and prosperous. This is obviously a wonderful thought. However, what has this Government done? The Conservative Government was the one that attempted to reduce old age security pensions through deindexation.
This is the Government that deindexed family allowances and that now wants to deindex the child tax credit. This is the Government that increased the sales tax for ordinary families in Canada.
What the Speech from the Throne says is not reassuring, and I quote:
Canadians would want their governments to give the highest priority in social policy to those who are in greatest need.
We agree up to a point. However, I am afraid that there is another message that can be found in the Speech from the Throne: that there will be an attack on universal social programs. Unfortunately, this is an objective of this Government, even though the Conservatives promised during the electoral campaign not to touch universal programs. They started doing so. Fortunately, under the pressure of Canadian men and women all over the country, the Government had to back down with respect to old age security pensions. Unfortunately, in spite of the efforts of women's groups, churches, unions, citizens all over the place, the pressure was not enough and the Government deindexed family allowances.
We in the NDP believe that we need universal programs. They should be the cornerstone of our system. Non universal programs are also most important, but we should not rely solely on those programs to ensure a decent living for Canadian families.

October 23, 1986
The Address-Ms. McDonald
Canadians want to see action on jobs. They want to see action on fair taxes, but we do not get action in this Speech from the Throne. The speech has high sounding phrases but we do not see specific promises that Canadians would like to have heard, such as, the Government is not going to appoint its friends to high places anymore. That kind of promise for real highness in action we do not see in the Speech from the Throne. There is rhetoric on tax reform, but I will believe it when I see it. Meanwhile, the shift to individual taxes from corporate taxes is continuing. We know that 79,000 corporations made a profit in Canada in 1985 but did not pay a dime in tax. There is nothing about that. There is nothing about seriously closing tax loopholes. We need specific action. Instead we have only a vague statement of achieving a better equilibrium between income tax and "other forms" of tax. What other forms, Mr. Speaker-sales taxes, excise taxes or corporate taxes?

We have to realize that tax loopholes are the main reason for the present deficit. If corporations had paid their fair share of taxes, we would have had sufficient funds for government spending. It is therefore vitally important to plug those loopholes if we want to come to grips with the accrued deficit.
The Speech from the Throne mentioned a reduction in the deficit. We should be aware, however, that it is only a reduction in the rate of growth of that deficit. It is not an absolute reduction. Our deficit has increased more under the present Government than under the previous one.
The Speech from the Throne proposes a forum on postsecondary education. No one can find fault with such an initiative, but we have to say that it is not good enough. Last spring, this same Government slashed the budgets of postsecondary education without consulting the provinces. The cuts made in post-secondary education budgets on that occasion are just the opposite of what the Conservatives promised during the election campaign when they pledged to increase the budgets of post-secondary education. Provinces and universities and colleges are expecting this Government to roll back its unilaterally imposed reductions.
There is at least one good thing for which I could congratulate the Government, the priority given to science and technology in the Speech from the Throne. That speech announced the appointment of a national advisory board for industrial technology, to be chaired by the Prime Minister himself.
The Speech from the Throne also mentions a billion dollars for scientific research. However, contrary to what the Speech says, it is not new money, but the same already announced in the spring, in a program condemned by scientists themselves as being impractical. This program to assist universities has- according to scientists, that I am inclined to believe-very
little chance of success. It requires private enterprise to provide funds to universities. However, there are no incentives for the companies to do so.

I would like to add that this encouragement of research is only in the field of the natural sciences and it excludes completely the social sciences and the humanities. They are part of Canada, an important part of the universities and colleges and an important part of Canadian life. They have been neglected in this Speech from the Throne.

This Speech from the Throne gave more space and more interest than usual to cultural matters, and this is also to the credit of the Government. It promises to strengthen our cultural institutions, and especially the broadcasting system. It makes a commitment to Canadian cultural values. But, this costs money. It is not possible to broadcast more Canadian programs without increasing the budget of the CBC. The Caplan-Sauvageau report is excellent and full of concrete recommandations to promote Canadian programmming. But, again, implementing these recommandations would cost money. The private sector has its own responsibilities, but we, in Parliament, are responsible for the CBC. We will have to provide more money if we want to achieve this goal of more Canadian programming.

This speech from the Throne includes some measures that are old, some that are new, some that are borrowed, some that are recycled-

speechtext:
Some of them are blue, indeed. Some of this Speech distinctly gave me that impression as I sat listening to it. Some measures represent reversals. I am pleased to see some of those that go backwards because they should not have been entered into in the first place.
When we add together all of these different kinds of measures in the Speech from the Throne, what do we get, Mr. Speaker? We have a speech with a lot of rhetoric, a lot of Tory objectives for the most part, and even where there is something questionable in the Speech from the Throne, such as, what I think is a veiled attack on the universal programs, it is very gently and civily put. It is not a direct attack on the social programs but a statement that something else should be done instead. This is a very civil Speech from the Throne. Nonetheless, it is not a good Speech from the Throne. It is not an effective Speech from the Throne. There are not enough concrete measures. It is not specific enough. There is no action in the Speech from the Throne. There is a false diagnosis of our problems and so there are false solutions to those problems.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned the problem of smoking and alcohol and I share her concerns, as she knows. I wonder what she would specifically propose that the Government do about the heroin problem which is so severe in the province in which she was born, British Columbia, and about the question of other illegal drugs. What specifically would she like to see the Government do concerning an industry which, as she knows, amounts to $9 billion or $10 billion a year in illegal sales to Canadians, particularly young people.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question. It is a subject on which I used to do some work. I was a research associate for the inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs some years ago and certainly the heroin question was very important. At that time there was considerable debate and it is ongoing. There are no answers with unanimous support from scientists or practitioners who work in this area. Methadone maintenance was certainly the fashionable solution at that time. It has had some success in Britain and it has certainly had some effect in cutting down on the black market. I do not know how appropriate a solution it is for Canada. There has also been the problem of that drug finding its way on to the streets. It is then perhaps the substitution of a less serious problem for a more serious problem, but it is not a solution in and of itself.
I would just say that we need to look at this question in a very broad context. Studies done for the Le Dain Commission showed, and they continue to be borne out, that the drug culture goes past legal and illegal boundaries. Anyone who uses one drug is more likely to use another drug. The more drugs one uses, even if they are legal drugs, even including tea or coffee, the more likely one is to use other drugs. That is not to say that people necessarily move all the way up the scale, but there is something of a drug culture and when people get into it and drugs become a solution for what is probably a human problem, then people are more likely to seek that out in other ways. I think we have to attack the idea that there is a chemical solution to human problems, and that is the way I would go after it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member with considerable care. I suppose it is inevitable that a member of the Opposition, after a Throne Speech is brought down, would attack it for being general and vague and pious and platitudinous, lacking in specifics and lacking in details. That is the formula response from an opposition Party. I suppose if the truth be known, when this Party was in Opposition we trotted out the same formula rhetoric.
The Address-Ms. McDonald

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We remember it.

speechtext:
That does not make it any more valid and its repetition this afternoon does not add any veracity to it.
I wonder if the Hon. Member appreciates what a Throne Speech is. It is not legislation. It is not a Budget. It is not an economic statement. It is an indication from the Government, through the voice of the Crown, of the path the Government intends to follow. It is not, to use the metaphore, a detailed road map.
She will know, since she read the Throne Speech carefully, that in the environmental field there were several iniatives which go well beyond the platitudinous. There was a firm commitment to bring in early, as a government-wide priority, a new Environmental Protection Act which will focus on toxic chemicals. Earlier this week in Ottawa I released some of the details of that Act, and before very long, in Parliament and outside, I will be sharing with the House and the public at large the legislation itself in draft form as a consultative tool.
The Throne Speech also makes a commitment to bring in the first major set of reforms to the National Parks Act since it was devised in 1930, some 56 years ago. That is a firm commitment, not just piety and not just platitudes.
I do not think the Hon. Member would have expected the Throne Speech to give chapter and verse about the Environmental Protection Act or the National Parks amendments, otherwise we would still be sitting in the Senate Chamber listening to Her Excellency reading the document. In so many areas touched upon in the Throne Speech we indicated where we are going and how we intend to get there, but obviously there was not room in such an institution as the Throne Speech to dot all the 'i's and cross all the 't's.
I am just wondering if the Hon. Member is appreciative of what a Throne Speech is. She indicated, I am sure unintentionally, that she had another vision of the institution than that which I have just described.

Mr. Speaker, I did not indicate that I had another vision, although I do in fact have one. I said I thought this was a Throne Speech without vision. Where it deals with the environment, I would commend the Minister. I think there are relatively concrete, relatively specific measures in the Throne Speech. The Minister will also know that in the time allotted to a Member, apart from the first three speakers, that being 20 minutes, it is not possible to deal with every aspect of the speech. The part dealing with the environment is one of the better parts of the speech. It takes us further from where we are now.
As to how specific the Speech from the Throne should be, that is a question of degree. Obviously it cannot include a detailed analysis of proposed legislation. No one would suggest that. I was simply expressing a disappointment that it was not more precise in stating what measures would be taken. I was disappointed that quite a bit of space was given to what I would call rhetoric. There were nice sounding phrases but no
