speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak in the Elouse for the first time not only on the Throne Speech but in this new session. I want to congratulate you on your reappointment as Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House. It is nice to see you back in the Chair.
I want to focus on the theme of science and technology as it relates to the Throne Speech. The riding I represent is a thriving technological community as well as having one of the leading educational and research institutions in North America, the University of Saskatchewan, in Saskatoon. I am delighted that this Government has demonstrated once again through a strong commitment that this issue is a priority. Having said that, I would like to commend the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) for his superb efforts in staying the course and fighting for scarce financial resources around the cabinet table.
I would first like to talk about the high technology community since that is an industrial sector which has had considerable impact on Saskatoon and whose success has been recognized in the Speech from the Throne. In Saskatchewan there is a clear recognition that industry is the driving force which pulls technology out of the labratory and launches it into the market-place. That is probably best demonstrated by the University of Saskatchewan and the private sector in Saskatoon which have been at the game of technology transfer now for probably 15 to 20 years, and I will expand on that in a few moments.
The City of Saskatoon, and my province in general, are well known for their creative and innovative entrepreneurs. To date, there are 164 high technology companies in Saskatchewan, which is an increase of 40 firms since 1982. There are over 90 technology firms in Saskatoon alone. This new development means the creation of hundreds of jobs. Saskatchewan technology firms have expanded their own sales substantially. For example, Develcon Electronics had $5 million worth of sales to NASA in one year and $4 million in sales to Lockheed Aircraft Corporation. SED Systems, which grew out of the University of Saskatchewan, had S19 million in sales of earth stations to Brazil. It had $26 million in sales on the Canadian Frigate Program. SCI-TEC, another company, had sales to Germany, India and the United Kingdom. Northern Telecom has its world fibre optics production and sales operation in Saskatoon, marketing that unique technology around the globe.
These people put new ideas to work, turn advanced technology into new products or processes and convert these into wealth through aggressive selling in very competitive markets. This can be done in an area of high cost. There is a great deal of financial risk in building an advanced technology business, but risk is what free enterprise is all about. The Government of Saskatchewan is a supportive partner of such entrepreneurs and shares in the financial risk of such ventures. That partnership between business and Government has rapidly made my province one of this continent's most attractive, advanced technology locations for innovators and investors.
Perhaps some people are wondering why I am not talking about our wheat and potash in Saskatchewan. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that things have changed in our province, thanks to some good leadership from Grant Devine's Government and thanks to a lot of people at the University of Saskatchewan and entrepreneurs who saw the challenge and certainly accepted it.
Communication is the key to implementing this partnership, especially in federal-provincial relations. For example, the new technology steering committee is responsible for the over-all co-operation of science and technology activities in Saskatchewan by the federal and provincial Governments. This is a positive enforcement that federal and provincial growth can be achieved by working together. I look forward to working with the re-elected Government of Grant Devine in the Province of Saskatchewan in the next four to five years. This committee was instrumental in co-ordinating and promoting funding decisions for research and infrastructure such as the CadCam Centre at the Saskatchewan Research Council, a proposed potash research centre, a microelectronics centre and others. Under the auspices of the committee, science and technology and DRIE have worked together to develop the ERDA subagreement on advanced technology which was signed in 1984. Again, this was the first one in Canada. The agreement will deliver $33.2 million over five years to accelerate the growth of Saskatchwan's advanced technology industries. Indeed, this is support to industrial and technological development and diversification in the west. It is an excellent vehicle for growth and development in the field of science and technology.
A new research infrastructure has been established to support advanced technology development in Saskatchewan through federal and provincial funding. Let me name a few key achievements. There is the Canadian Centre of Instrumentation which has allocated $1 million over the next five years to the Saskatchewan Research Council. The National Plant Biotechnology Centre recently opened a capital project of $6 million, with $2.4 million of operating funding. This is located in Saskatoon and is the only centre in the country that is doing research in the area of agricultural biotechnology which probably holds some of the new technology that will lead us into diversification of our current wheat and barley crops. There is the western Centre of Toxicology, with a $2 million capital expansion at the University of Saskatchewan. There is
October 23, 1986

the Linear Accelerator Laboratory expansion at the University of Saskatchewan for just under $6 million. There is the National Centre of Hydrology which I had the pleasure of opening on behalf of the Minister just a matter of weeks ago. This is a $17 million facility that was built on the campus of the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. Many exciting things are happening in this area thanks to the co-operative efforts of this Government and the Province of Saskatchewan.
For more years than I can imagine, businessmen have continued to look, not to the provinces but to Ottawa for leadership in science and technology development, and for support in creating an environment that is conducive to success in R and D. Deaf ears were turned to such enterprises prior to September, 1984 but, as the Speech from the Throne confirms, now Canada has a Government and a Prime Minister committed to scientific and technological development.
In addition, the Government supports science and technology through activities such as tax incentives for industrial research and development amounting to some $500 million annually, federal-provincial sub-agreements on science and technology amounting to $100 million over the next five years, and other sub-agreements with science and technology content amounting to $327 million over the next few years.
The Conservative Government used its common sense when it eliminated the Scientific Research Tax Credit in the May, 1985 Budget. Indeed, the Liberals introduced the SRTC in 1973 to encourage scientific research. It proved to be an expensive program characterized by abuse because research was so ill defined. The Liberals failed to establish a pre-audit or approval process. Without built in security measures, the program was open for this kind of abuse.
The Government is acting in other areas to improve the fairness and effectiveness of the tax system to safeguard and ensure that tax rules are not used in inappropriate ways to avoid taxes. Instead of abusing the system, the Government introduced more effective and better targeted provisions to support research and development.
The federal Government is the single largest financial contributor to science and technology in Canada. The Government has announced in the Throne Speech an initiative that will provide $1 billion in new funding for science research over the next five years. This funding will focus on many things, including research and co-ordination between universities and the private sector. I can assure you that the University of Saskatchewan and the many small scientific research companies will look forward to sharing in some of that funding.
We spent $4.2 billion on science and technology in 1985-86. These activities support a number of objectives, including industrial development, protection of the environment, health and safety of Canadians, national security, and basic scientific research. These are all positive steps to strengthen science and technology's role in creating jobs and improving the quality of life for Canadians. That is what I call a commitment.
The Address-Mr. Ravis
Those are not just my sentiments, Mr. Speaker, they are the feelings of a number of journalists and high technology experts. For example, our great newspaper friends at the Toronto Star have written: "No Canadian Prime Minister has ever made this kind of personal commitment to promoting high technology development". Roy MacGregor of The Ottawa Citizen called the Throne Speech: "An imaginative and welcome announcement that this country now agrees with the rest of the world in acknowledging the value of research and development".
I want to indicate that approximately a year ago I was invited with a number of my colleagues from the science and technology caucus committee to attend a dinner at one of the larger embassies in Ottawa. After completing our meal we were asked to discuss Canada's science and technology policy. I must say that it was embarrassing for us to say that the previous Government had not really developed a policy and that we were just in the process of developing one in the next couple of years.
In general, Canada's high technology industry reacted favourably to the four point platform increasing support to science and technology. A national advisory board for industrial technology, chaired by the Prime Minister-a first for any Government-and composed of some of Canada's leading industrialists and scientists will definitely raise the profile of leading technology initiatives. This committee will assess national science and technology goals and policies, and their application to Canada's economy. The Government will seek to achieve high standards of excellence in education, technology development, and innovation. The introduction of a new federal science and technology strategy, building on the initiatives undertaken to date, will encourage necessary reforms within federal administration to promote Canada's international competitiveness. For example, international exchanges have been initiated with a number of countries, including Japan, the United States, China, Australia, and western European countries.
The Government will also convene a national conference on techology and innovation to assist Canada to define new technology goals. This is what I call leadership. Research has always been intact but the development end has been lacking in the past. That point was well put to me at a dinner I attended in Saskatoon recently. A number of people from the business sector did not complain so much about research and development; they said the research was being done, but we were not spending enough money on the development side of the equation. It is all a matter of marketing and manufacturing our technology, getting the research off the shelf.
Canadians should be proud of our technological goals and achievement which this Government is committed to development. The Canadian Advanced Technology Association applauded the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for "committing his own time to assessing and setting national policy".

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Ravis
However, Mr. Speaker, even a group of high technology experts like those in the Canadian Advanced Technology Association will admit that industry cannot be driven by Government alone. Success in such a competitive field depends on a number of factors, but especially on a strong and vibrant university research community. Without such a community, much of the pure research which eventually results in marketable products and processes would never occur. I know as well from my experience in Saskatoon that without universities, industry would never have a steady group of highly qualified young men and women to fulfil its personal requirements.
University research has been a priority of this Government and also a priority of the Progressive Conservative Government which was led by the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). In 1979, the Clark Government gave stability and consistency to the budgets of the three university research granting councils. Not surprisingly, this commitment was forgotten by the Liberal Government which followed, which continues to press the Government today for policies that it never thought of initiating in its own 20 years in office.
In February of this year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) restored that principle and established a five-year plan of consistent funding for these granting councils. No previous Government has given the granting councils such a solid commitment. Not only that, the Minister also committed the federal Government to matching the private sector's funding of university research on a dollar-for-doliar basis up until 1991. This will mean up to $.75 billion of increased research funding for Canada's universities.
This strong commitment to research and development is a clear and positive signal for Canada's university community. It is a plan which provides much needed new funds for university research and also builds a bridge between the demands of industry and the skills of university students and professors. No longer will a potentially lucrative mechanism or process sit on the shelf of a university or Government research laboratory. Technology will now be defused and applied to industrial needs in a way which is mutually lucrative and supportive without hindering the advancement of basic science.
The Government firmly believes that putting more money into R and D at the university level is an investment in the future of Canada. The University of Saskatchewan has previously been a leader in establishing partnerships with the local high technology sector. As I mentioned earlier, SED Systems in Saskatoon is probably one of the best examples. It employs hundreds and hundreds of people and is involved in some very interesting programs, including space research.
The Government's initiative will only serve to augment the university's efforts. I am sure other Hon. Members who are fortunate to have universities in their ridings will find this to be the case as well. The matching formula, coupled with the initiatives noted in the Speech from the Throne, is a clear demonstration of the Government's commitment to research and its sensitivity to technological change. Technological
change is pertinent to our survival and illustrates progress in our record of economic renewal.
A healthy economic future has been initiated throughout the country. In particular, our Government has enhanced job opportunities for our youth. There is a decline in youth unemployment. The task is by no means completed. There is still much to do in the area of youth unemployment. But it is encouraging to see that youth unemployment has dropped almost three points since we have come to office. More programs will be introduced to promote entreneurship amongst our youth.
All these commitments to R and D, linking job promotion for youth, are stepping stones to improve employment prospects as well as our standard of living. Once again, this is leadership through commitment, consultation and co-operation; indeed, a process for growth. In these steps to restructure our economy, we must all work together. The Government has clearly demonstrated its ability to work in co-operation with industry, universities and provinces in enhancing Canada's industrial strength in partnership with our young Canadian researchers.
In closing, I would like to say that these benefits can be shared by all Canadians. When we talk about research and development, we are not just talking about scientists and technicians. We are talking about all the jobs which spin off, from secretaries to people in the service industries. I think it is important that we understand that this is something which has value for every Canadian, union people, non-union people, technicians and scientists. This partnership can only mean a healthy economic future for all of my constituents in Saskatoon and for the country in general.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly wish to address the issue raised by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins). She has many professors and staff members from the University of British Columbia and Simon Fraser University living in her riding. These people have a very keen interest in this issue. In all fairness, the Government could have come in with a science and technology policy or a change in that regard in September of 1984. In other words, let us not look at what the
The Address-Mr. Ravis
problem is and how serious it is, let us just act on it. Rather than doing that, the Government decided it wanted to try to reach some consensus out there in the country, because there was a fear that there was a great deal of duplication, as there so often is when federal flags and provincial flags are being waved. There was talk of a White Paper on science and technology being brought down in the House this fall. One other subject I would like to elaborate on is that the establishment of a Standing Committee on Science and Technology has been beneficial to Members of the House of Commons. This is the first time that the subject has been given such priority.
To conclude, the Hon. Member asked me how long I think it will take. I think we are very close. I think we are possibly as close as four to six months in terms of coming out with a policy which will recognize all of the talking and consulting that has gone on in the country over the last two years.

the University of Saskatchewan and the University of Regina. I might add that this has been as a result of technological assistance and expertise that has come from the universities. subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in the House to speak to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. First of all, I want to congratulate the Speaker and all other Members who will have the honour of sitting in the Chair during this session. I also would like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to greet the people of the beautiful riding of Bourassa, and a special greeting to the people of Montreal North.
Mr. Speaker, the second session of the 33rd Parliament started with the customary Speech from the Throne, which
October 23, 1986

contains the new objectives of the Government of the day. But does it? Is this an original, brand-new Speech from the Throne? Or is it a Speech from the Throne full of recycled leftovers, reflecting the true nature and substance of a Conservative Government in its decline?
The Conservative Government has declined to the point that it needed a whole month to recycle the contents of its 1984 election platform. We recall, and all Canadians will recall, those pretty speeches and the 300 or so promises they made during the election campaign. What became of them? The people of Canada are not easily fooled. They can see through the tricks and trumpery of the Government opposite. And that is why the people in the riding of Bourassa and the people of Canada are wondering what will happen to the promises made in this Throne Speech.
Mr. Speaker, this Speech from the Throne mentions social justice. How can they talk about social justice? How can they talk about their social policy? Does this Government really think Canadians believe the Conservatives when they claim to be the party of social justice?
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not easily fooled. A Government that has managed to reduce indexation of family allowances, cut back on the increases for transfer payments made to the provinces for education and health care, cut unemployment insurance benefits for thousands of Canadians who receive severance pay or early retirement pensions and who are still looking for employment, a Government that attempted to de-index Old Age Security pensions-and they call that social justice, Mr. Speaker, when they want to deindex Old Age Security pensions?
And speaking of Old Age Security pensions, Mr. Speaker, my riding of Montreal-Bourassa has large population of senior citizens. I am constantly fighting to defend their rights and I will continue to do so. Many senior citizens in Montreal North know how I respect and sympathize with them. Other people have tried to get at the senior citizens, but I won't name names in the House. The people who wanted to disturb the tranquility and peace of mind of these senior citizens know to whom I am referring and I don't have to name them in these precincts.
Mr. Speaker, this kind of Government cannot claim to be a Government that promotes social justice. It is a Government that takes from the poor and gives to the rich. When I say it takes from the poor and gives to the rich, I think a good example is non-taxable capital gains. This Government cannot afford to talk about economic justice, and Canadians know this only too well. They no longer have any confidence in this Government, after only two years in power.
Mr. Speaker, this Government is synonymous with wasting money and wasting time. Canadians have seen through the tricks of the Conservative Government, as indicated by the polls they are so fond of quoting. Take the results of the last poll published on October 6, which inform us that the majority
The Address-Mr. Rossi
of Canadians no longer have any confidence in the Government opposite. According to this poll, about 52 per cent of Canadians do not approve of the Conservative Government's policies. Not only has every Canadian or just about lost all confidence in this Conservative Government, Mr. Speaker, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has also lost all credibility in this great country of Canada. I think that this is a rather serious matter, Mr. Speaker.
However, how could it be otherwise? The Conservative Party and this Government are without meaning and without any substance. The Speech from the Throne is a perfect example of a speech where appearances are more important than the substance, if there is any substance, a speech full of illusions which could become real only in a dreamworld.
Mr. Speaker, we Canadians live in a real world, in a country with problems which require real and practical solutions, but this Conservative Government is unable to understand this, let alone find these solutions.
Each day, the Members opposite ask us: What would you do? What would you do in such or such a case? However, it is you, Government Members, who must say what you would do, not us.
The Speech from the Throne is the proof that this Government has no action plan, that it is interested only in short term political and economic problems and that it cannot take its responsibilities and try to provide a clear direction for this country. Mr. Speaker, Canadians have had enough of Conservatives who can only make irresponsible promises, of actions which most often result in scandals, ministerial resignations and broken promises. As evidence, we have only to look at the bank failures under a Conservative Government.
We are telling this Government that Canadians no longer have any confidence in the Progressive Conservative Party. As I said earlier, Canadians no longer believe their high-flown and irresponsible promises. Canadians no longer believe that this Government has the authority, the respect and the ability required to govern Canada as it deserves.
Mr. Speaker, there are in my riding a great many senior citizens who are worried and concerned about the promises made by this Conservative Government and their decisions which are, as everybody knows, totally contradictory. They certainly remember and will remember, come election time, everything which could have happened to them. They have been duped. They have been deceived by this Government which would have them believe that this Throne Speech is better than that of 1984. It is not. One need only check what happened in 1985-86 to the unemployment insurance benefits for people on early retirement.
Why has the Government not accepted the proposal made by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner)? Why has not the Government entertained an adequate and realistic policy for golden agers in the areas of health care, shelters,

October 23, 1986
The Address-Mr. Boyer
long-term care, community homes, lodging subsidies, as well as a home services scheme?
Mr. Speaker, senior citizens are a political force in Canada, as the Conservative Party painfully realized in 1982 and will painfully realize again come election time.
Mr. Speaker, there were by-elections in Saint-Maurice and Pembina recently. If they have made an objective analysis of these by-election results, Members of the Progressive Conservative Party certainly realize that they have lost a major part of their electoral support. Mr. Speaker, these results have been brought about by two years of inconsistency in power and foolish promises.
For that matter, the Prime Minister's decision to transfer the construction of a prison from Drummondville to his own riding will do nothing to improve this Government's credibility. His decision will certainly not change the opinion of the Drummondville people.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) would not speak out and oppose the Prime Minister's decision to move this prison from his riding of Drummondville to the riding of the Prime Minister?
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Drummondville had originally been selected as the site for that prison. It met with the criteria, and it was meant to complete the existing institution.
How much will this cost Canadians, Mr. Speaker? It will cost them $16 million more, $16 million to boost the image and popularity of this Prime Minister who has lost all credibility. Canadians are finding this a little expensive. Would it be in order to boost his prestige with the people in Schefferville? Why is that prison built in Port-Cartier, Mr. Speaker? Would it be to somehow repair the damage? How can the Prime Minister try to have people gobble that one up, Mr. Speaker? By dangling those 37 or 38 per cent unemployment figures in Port-Cartier. But all Hon. Members in this House know very well that is false, utterly false. The unemployment rate in Port-Cartier is around 15 per cent.
And please do not try to convince the people in Port-Cartier that this will be creating prison guards' jobs in that great 1 prison which will be built in Port-Cartier. Let people in Port- j Cartier come and tell me how many guards' jobs this will ' create in their constituency. Let them also come and tell me how many guards were transferred from another prison to go to Port-Cartier. Do not fool yourselves, people of Port-Cartier. Do not fool yourselves. That will be no job creation exercise. Do come and tell me the number of guards who will be hired from the constituency of Port-Cartier for service in that prison.
I am telling you, it is my humble belief that guards will be transferred from other prisons in the Province of Quebec to Port-Cartier, rather than new jobs being created. Do not be fooled by the Prime Minister.
And before this goes on, I would like the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault), the Member for Drummond who rises more often than not to speak about everything but real
issues to rise and uphold his rights. Now is the time, Mr. Member for Drummond, to fight for your people in Drummondville. Now is the time, Mr. Member for Drummond, to bring spin-offs if any to your constituency. Now is the time to get a move on. Now is the time to speak to your Prime Minister. Now is the time to rise in this House.
This might be an entertaining scenario, Mr. Speaker, but when we remember these are the kind of people who are at the helm, it is enough to make you cry.
By its very nature, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne is an important document which should reflect the Government's social, political and economic policies, and indicate how they are going to be achieved. No, Sir, I think we have here a text of great literary value which does not spell anything out, which fails to advocate political solutions, all told a document totally devoid of meaning, vigour and realism. As we happen to know the authors, Mr. Speaker, we should not be surprised.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am a Liberal, I belong to the Official Opposition. I am the elected representative of the constituency of Bourassa and, as such, I urge the Prime Minister and his colleagues to change their attitute towards Canadians and not take them as the average Joes on which to try various policies for size, as the Government may see fit.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are very serious and responsible people, and when they realize they are being led by an irresponsible Government they have every right to feel they have been let down and led astray, so they react.
Witness their reaction to the recent by-elections, and there will be more of the same next time around.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, talking about the next election, a moment ago I was listening to my colleague from Lachine (Mr. Layton) who was saying that, before the 1984 election, the people of Lachine wanted a change, and the sooner the better. All I can say to the Hon. Member is that he ought to travel around a bit, not only in his riding of Lachine but throughout the 282 constituencies of this beautiful country and he will see just how much Canadians want a change, a real change this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to many of the comments during the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne I was thinking of the public musings of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) of not many days ago, that the problem with a Throne Speech is that by its nature it is given to general statements. Perhaps he was somewhat on the mark. The criticism I have been hearing of the Government's program, policy, and action to date, based upon the Throne Speech and the comments coming from the other side of the House, is that it is all too vague and too general.
October 23, 1986

For example, in her remarks this afternoon the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) down played the Government's statement in the Throne Speech dealing with the drug crisis. Yet, several days after the Throne Speech, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) rose in the House and outlined in great detail very concrete steps which would be taken. Similarly, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) talked about ways in which the Government would enact legislation to see that the profits now being made in Canada through illicit drug trafficking, some $7 billion to $10 billion each year, would be recoverable by the Crown. These are very significant steps. They are part of a positive response to the issues.
It is folly to think that general statements contained in a Throne Speech to outline the general thrust of the Government are the be-all and end-all of the program. The criticism which has been coming at the Government based upon the Throne Speech is falling far short of the mark. It does not accurately and reasonably deal with the broad course upon which the Government has set itself.
When I talk about the broad course, perhaps I would be permitted a moment or two to say what I think it involves. In 1984, when Canadians decided to change the Government in Ottawa, those of us who came to form and support the new Government found that there were two really deep-seated problems in Ottawa. One of them was that financially the Government of Canada was running out of control. It was like a locomotive with a full head of steam that had somehow come off the rails. We have talked about the deficit. Every debate in the House has had a lot of content relating to deficit reduction, whether cuts or reductions which were being proposed were appropriate. Very often we heard Hon. Members opposite bemoaning cuts and efforts to get the deficit under control, even though there is no alternative.
However, dealing with the deficit was only one of two very basic problems. I submit that in fact there was another major problem, equally deep-seated, concerning the philosophy which had developed in Ottawa over the previous 10 years to 20 years. Let us call it the "Ottawa mind-set". What did the Ottawa mind-set or the Ottawa philosophy hold? This attitude permeated not only the Cabinet of the previous Government but right down through the Public Service.
I think we can perhaps see three elements in the Ottawa mind-set. First, it said that Ottawa knows best, that the banks of the Rideau River and of the Ottawa River are where the great wisdom of Canada is reposited. That is why, for example, it was never possible for resources offshore Newfoundland to be developed in a way that was important for Newfoundlanders-Ottawa knew best.
The second component of the mind-set was that the problems of the country could be solved by throwing money at them or by spending money. Of course that was a contributing factor to the large debt with which the country is still saddled.
The Address-Mr. Boyer
The third component of the Ottawa mind-set was that if we could not solve a problem by throwing money at it, we could solve it by regulating it, by establishing a board or commission, by enacting further requlations, or by bringing about the kinds of things we saw in the National Energy Program, for example. Those were the three components-Ottawa knows best, solve the problems by throwing money at them or, if that failed to work, regulate it.
Those three ideas formed a philosophy, attitude, or approach which so permeated the operations of the federal Government that we have had a very serious problem over the past two years, since coming here as a new Government, to try to effect the change Canadians clearly want in overcoming that fundamental hurdle. It is far more difficult than the deficit because it is much harder to deal with the ideas which people carry in their minds. We are dealing with nothing less than a matter of changing attitudes.
I should like to note that in The Gazette of Montreal today, the editors provided two cheers for the Conservative Government. No editorial board would ever give three cheers for a Government, or there would be something totally wrong with them. It reads:
Two cheers to the Mulroney Government for earning praise from Auditor General Kenneth Dye after his sharp-pencilled review of the first full year of the Government's operations.
The Auditor General, an habitual scourge of government management, hailed the present Government for "bringing a sense of better management to the Public Service." Changing Ottawa's psychology of spending is a large Tory achievement.
Those were not the comments of a Member on the government side of the House. Those were the comments of the editorial board of The Gazette. They referred to "changing Ottawa's psychology of spending". It is evidence of what I am talking about when I say that the big battle before us is changing attitudes which are entrenched here.
I should like to refer to another problem. In dealing with many issues, Hon. Members opposite have been particularly interested in focusing on what I would call the small details or trivial matters. For example, the recent trip of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to Asia saw major accomplishments-the admission of Canada to the Group of Seven, agricultural issues being placed on the agenda for the first time, and significant developments in trade with China and other Pacific Rim countries. What have we heard about from the Opposition on those matters? They asked the following questions. What did the butler do? Did the butler do it? They went from the sublime to the ridiculous. Some members of the Liberal caucus might want to write a book on, did the butler do it? The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is no longer as much the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition as he is chairman of the Book-of-the-Month Club. The Liberal caucus is spewing out books at an incredible rate. Some of them are fine reading. I am sure the next book to come out will be called "Opposition Members Handbook to the Game of Trivial Pursuit". There has been so much noisy and disputatious comment coming from across the way that Canadians

October 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
have had their attention diverted from some of the more serious matters affecting the Government.
In conclusion, there are four great areas in which the Government has set long-term action. There is the possibility of a new bilateral trade treaty with the United States. Reform of the tax system is now under way. The Government is dealing with regional development and disparities in a broad fashion and is generally dealing with the whole question of deficit reduction. Those four broad areas have set us on the right course.
I am happy to have had a chance to put my views on the record during this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-TAKEOVER OF CONTINENTAL BANK. (B) REPAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA ADVANCES
BANKS AND BANKING-TAKEOVER OF CONTINENTAL BANK. (B) REPAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA ADVANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 9 and 16 I asked questions about the Government's approval of the takeover of the Continental Bank, which is a Canadian bank, by Lloyd's Bank, which is British owned. This takeover was unprecedented. As Members will know, it was not an outright takeover but an exchange of assets and liabilities in accordance with existing provisions of the Bank Act. My concern is not specifically with the details of this transaction. I am more concerned with the fact that yet again the Government has put itself in the position of having to make important, precedent-setting decisions involving financial institutions without the benefit of a policy framework.
For two years now, we have been hearing that the Government considers it a priority to update the legislation regulating banks, trust companies, insurance companies and the securities industry. There is no disagreement that new legislation is badly needed. Yet, after two years of Conservative Government, we are awash in studies and really no further ahead in terms of legislation in place than we were two years ago.
Concern has grown as over the past two years banks and trust companies have failed, a major non-financial corporation took control of Canada's largest trust company, a foreign-owned bank acquired ownership of a Canadian bank, and, in every instance, the Government was forced to act in an ad hoc way, flying by the seat of its pants because it did not have legislation in place to deal with the situation.
What is even more worrisome is that the longer the Government delays in bringing forward its proposals for legislation, the fewer options it will have. By delaying and allowing the industry and provincial Governments to take the lead, the Government is reducing its room to manoeuvre and is fast running out of policy options and time. All Canadians have an interest in how their financial institutions are regulated by government. Whether we speak of entrepreneurs and business people looking for capital investment, people looking to take out a mortgage or renew a mortgage, anyone shopping for a loan, or anyone with money in a savings account or RRSP, we all have an interest in knowing that the Government is acting to ensure that the rapid evolution in the financial services industry works for Canada and Canadians. Right now we do not have that assurance because we do not have legislation to give the Government any kind of a handle on the situation.
The question of ownership of financial institutions, for example, has come up with some regularity. Earlier this year the Government approved the industrial giant Imasco's takeover of Genstar Corporation, which owned Canada's largest trust company. At that time, the former Minister of State for Finance was quoted in The Financial Times as having said that:
-she had no difficulty with industrial groups controlling financial institutions.
That, Mr. Speaker, was April 5, 1986. Now there is a new Minister, and this Minister is quoted as having said:
I have great problems with the notion of non-financial institutions controlling financial institutions.
That is from The Financial Post of September 20, 1986. So there is really no telling where the Government stands on the issue of ownership. We just have to wait for the legislation which, as I am sure we are about to be told, will be introduced very shortly. That statement would carry a great more impact if we had not heard it so often in the last two years.
Tomorrow the Government will be tabling the report of the Estey Commission on bank failures and the regulation of the banking industry. I look forward to seeing that report and debating the legislation which I hope will follow before the Government is further overtaken either by events in the industry or the regulatory initiatives of other governments.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-TAKEOVER OF CONTINENTAL BANK. (B) REPAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA ADVANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after several months of negotiations, the Continental Bank of Canada and the Lloyds Bank of London announced on October 2 that they had come to an
October 23, 1986

agreement under which the Lloyds Bank of Canada, the Canadian subsidiary of the London bank, would acquire the majority of the assets of the Continental Bank and take over the majority of its liabilities.
This agreement was the result of the efforts made by the Continental these last few months to find a major banking institution with which to merge. One year ago, following the closing of the two Western Canadian banks, the Continental Bank unfortunately had to face substantial fund withdrawals by commercial and institutional depositors even though it was financially healthy.
The bank had to rely to a great extent on the Bank of Canada and the mechanisms offered by the major banks to replace the lost deposits. While the Continental was making progress in re-establishing the confidence of depositors and reducing its need for advances from the Bank of Canada, as the Hon. Member probably knows, its management was aware that a complete recovery would take a lot of time. To ensure that the operations of the bank could be carried out in the future in the best interests of its customers, depositors and employees, the management decided that the best solution was to join forces with a major international bank such as Lloyds.
While the Government was kept informed of the progress made in the negotiations and while it supported the efforts made by the Continental to come to an agreement, the Government itself did not initiate the negotiations. The agreement is strictly an initiative of the private sector. I repeat to the Hon. Member that the agreement is strictly an initiative of the private sector.
The transaction complies fully with the banking legislation, and as far as possible, all available information has been provided to Parliament and the public. The Minister of State for Finance has already appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to answer questions on the transaction.
As for the question about the advances, I would like to emphasize that, to ensure a harmonious transfer of the operations of the Continental Bank, the advances granted to the Continental by the Bank of Canada will be replaced by advances to Lloyds. Lloyds has agreed to reimburse the Bank of Canada within a reasonably short period, that is no longer than three months after completing its transaction with the Continental. This extension should help Lloyds find proper funding in an orderly fashion and lessen possible disturbances on monetary markets. Finally, I should like to take this opportunity to repeat the firm commitment made by the Government to amend the regulations applying to the financial sector. Our aim is to ensure consumer protection and enhance the integrity of the Canadian financial system which, as it should be noted, is one of the best in the world. The financial sector reform is a high priority for this Government and new legislation will be introduced as soon as possible.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEPARTMENTAL ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REFORM. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEPARTMENTAL ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REFORM. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the House briefly on the subject of mismanagement and maladministration in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Many shocking revelations have come to light recently with respect to the operations and functions of that Department within the region of Manitoba. So bad was the situation of the Department's activities in that region that the Government felt obliged to take action.
The former Minister called for an outside audit, which resulted in the Currie Report. The Currie Report confirmed the allegations of the southern chiefs that the Manitoba region was maladministered and that the bands were paying a very heavy price in terms of the quality of services they were able to deliver to their people. These responsibilities had been transferred to them, but they lacked the wherewithal to provide a level of service that would be regarded as acceptable.
Further allegations and charges from the Manitoba region led the present Minister to call for an investigation by the RCMP into the activities of the Manitoba region. This was serious business. Further allegations followed that and, in answer to questions that I raised in the House, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) said that Treasury Board would undertake a financial review of the Manitoba region of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
We have had some action but, meanwhile, a large number of bands-some 30 or more-are in debt and are unable to serve their people.
I have argued consistently that the problem within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is not merely a problem in the Manitoba region. If it were just an isolated problem, then everything that the previous Minister and the present Minister are doing would probably be acceptable, provided that those bands could somehow be helped out of their indebtedness. However, the problem is more widespread.
This problem exists throughout the country, in every region, in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I suggest that right here in the headquarters in Ottawa there is also serious mismanagement and maladministration. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that recently a former employee of that Department revealed that he worked in a division known as the Audit Division? There were 17 so-called auditors in that division and seven support staff. The total payroll of that little group was $900,000, or almost $1 million. The surprising fact is that they do not do any auditing.
What do they do? They seek auditors in the private sector auditors who will take on contracts to audit some particular

October 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
project under the administration of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, These 17 people, many of whom are not qualified to be auditors, occasionally break away from their crossword puzzles or articles from the library to phone the private contractor who has been hired to do a certain audit to ask how it is going, if progress is being made and whether they can expect to hear something soon. In one year, 1985 to the present time, more than $2 million worth of auditing business from that Audit Division has been given to the private sector. These 17 people are only responsible for letting these contracts. That is maladministration.
If these charges were simply made by former employees of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, or if these charges were simply made by this little band of Opposition Members who are valiantly fighting for good government, and that was as far as it went, perhaps the Government would be able to say that is what it expects to hear.
Recently we had confirmation of this charge of mismanagement and maladministration from no less a person than the most important servant of Parliament, the Auditor General. He has revealed in his recent report that the Department of Indian Affairs is a hopeless wasteland of confusion. It lacks clear policies and directions. The Department is torn between an antiquated and authoritarian statute of this House called the Indian Act on the one hand and on the other hand, there is the pull and attraction of leaders from the indigenous communities who are saying there has to be a better way. There has to be some way in which they can establish a new kind of working relationship with the Government of Canada. There has to be some way in which nearly half a million people can once and for all cease being depressed, colonized and dealt with as if they had no intelligence or capability to look after their own day-to-day affairs in their communities.
These people want to become partners in Confederation. They are sick unto death, Sir, of being pushed to the outer fringes of society and maltreated by Government after Government. This is not just a condemnation of the present Government because this has been going on for a very long period of time.
In response to what the Auditor General has revealed, the Minister has called for a major review of the Department's management of lands, revenues and trust functions. I have no argument with the Minister in what he is doing, but it does not go far enough. We have to go much further.
The answer to what we have to do lies in the meetings of the First Ministers in April of next year when we write into the Constitution of this country the right of Indian people and indigenous people to manage, govern and control their own affairs. Then we begin to negotiate bilaterally arrangements and agreements for carrying out the responsibilities, and these we will honour. We will keep our word and break the pattern
of broken promises, broken treaties and failing the first citizens of the first nations of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEPARTMENTAL ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REFORM. (B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the honesty of the Hon. Member in saying this problem has been going on for a long, long time. In answer to the Hon. Member's question, let us recall the chronology of events in Manitoba which have led to the current allegations in the press of mismanagement and the response of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight).
In March of 1986, the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development commissioned a special investigation because of allegations made by the Brotherhood of First Nations. The Ward Mallette report was submitted on June 9, 1986. A departmental response was released on August 20, 1986. It responded in detail to the findings contained in the Ward Mallette special investigation.
On October 8, 1986, the Director of Finance for the Manitoba region resigned and took with him documents which he alleges support the Indians' concerns regarding underfunding, mismanagement and misleading of Parliament. He also alleged that activities of a criminal nature were taking place.
On October 9, 1986, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development asked the RCMP to investigate the allegations of wrongdoing referred to by Mr. MacPhee. Further, on October 15, 1986, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to undertake a comprehensive review of the Financial operations of the Department's regional office in Manitoba. Detailed departmental action plans have been developed and are being implemented to remedy those issues identified in the Manitoba special investigation.
In order to improve communications, the Minister has also agreed to meet with Chiefs on a periodic basis to discuss their concerns face-to-face in a business-like way. He recently signed a memorandum of understanding with 40 bands in northern Manitoba establishing such a process.
On August 27, 1986, in Winnipeg, the Minister made a commitment to the southern Chiefs of Manitoba that departmental officials were prepared to meet with bands on a case-by-case basis, if necessary, to discuss individual band indebtedness problems. As of this date, 39 of Manitoba's 60 bands have debts that require debt-recovery plans.
The Minister has asked that documents or evidence showing that contractual commitments have not been met should be presented to him. The Minister has also said unequivocally that where mistakes have been made, they will be corrected; where financial commitments have been entered into, they will be honoured.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) REDUCTION OF FRANCOPHONE EMPLOYEES (B) POLICY RELATING TO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) REDUCTION OF FRANCOPHONE EMPLOYEES (B) POLICY RELATING TO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the question I put to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) on October 16 of this year, which concerned a publication called Pony Express, published by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, where we read that the policy to reduce the number of Francophones within the RCMP is an official policy, and I wanted to know whether the Minister and his Government had approved or supported this position.
To situate the issue, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the need to protect language rights at the RCMP is nothing new. I certainly did not make it up since, in his 1985 report, the Commissioner of Official Languages remarked, and I quote:
"Where official languages are concerned, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has a long way to go before its troubles are over. Its review of language policy threatens to slow the current pace of reform even further."
This was back in 1985, Mr. Speaker, so the Commissioner of Official Languages was predicting what might happen at the RCMP.
And that is exactly what we are seeing today, Mr. Speaker, if we are to believe the press and if we listen carefully to what the Minister says. In The Globe and Mail of October 16, we read that it is officially accepted policy that the percentage of Francophones within the RCMP will be reduced from 20.8 per cent to 14.1 per cent. And in the same article we read that Mr. William Spring, assigned to the Official Languages Program with the RCMP, wrote, and I quote:

The 14 per cent Francophone ratio is a more realistic policy.

Mr. Speaker, this statement was made by the officer responsible for official languages, following a series of discussions between Treasury Board and the RCMP. I imagine it has a measure of credibility, because there was an exchange of correspondence which we have here today and to which I have referred in the House, where we can read ... and I want to quote the last paragraph of a letter signed by Mr. Aquilina, not just anybody, who was responsible for official languages at Treasury Board, and I quote verbatim:

Finally, I would like to suggest, given the importance of the proposed changes, that we proceed on the understanding that a re-assessment of the situation could be made after two years or so. Since it was agreed, at the January 10th meeting, that it would be to our mutual advantage to formalize the agreements reached

Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, it looks like a firm agreement in principle was finalized.
The Commissioner of Official Languages said in his 1985 report, and I quote: " The high percentage of Anglophone officers can be explained by the fact that nearly 85% work in the West." However, he qualifies these remarks, Mr. Speaker, and I quote again: "However, the question of geographical distribution should not make the RCMP lose sight of the fact that it is a national agency which should reflect the linguistic duality of Canada."
Mr. Speaker, "to reflect the fact that the RCMP is a national agency", I think the target of 20.8 per cent Francophones within the corps, the regular constabulary of the RCMP, would seem an acceptable minimum. And that was in fact the target agreed upon between the parties at the time, that is, the Liberal Government, the RCMP and Treasury Board.
So what is the Conservative Government doing with this problem? He says that there have been discussions, that these were unsatisfactory and that no official decision has been made. Again today the Minister told me there is no formal agreement, that if things do change he and his Government will continue to promote both official languages in the public service, and that he will make sure no attempt is made at reducing staff.
But, Mr. Speaker, it seems this is what they want to do through the back door. I do not care much for this because the House is about to consider serious amendments to the Official Languages Act which was adopted by the House in 1969 and which has not been amended in a significant way in almost 18 years.
When we ask the Minister what is going on with respect to the official languages we are told to be patient. When we ask the Minister to provide explanations about such important news as that mentioned in the RCMP Pony Express we are told there are discussions among civil servants. My God! Mr. Speaker, what are civil servants doing other than implementing the policies of this Government? What do civil servants do? Do they get a kick exchanging letters and documents, when they should be busy following up on the policies of the Government and advising its officials on how to proceed? I am somewhat concerned to hear the Government say: No, no, no. We wash our hands off. Like Pontius Pilate. We have nothing to do with this. Then in turn the civil servants say: Yes! Negotiations are under way and serious recommendations have been made.
Mr. Speaker, this evening I direct my question to the Parliamentary Secretary, in the hope that the Government will clear up the air and tell us in no uncertain terms: No! There is

October 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
no policy aimed at cutting down the staff. No! We do not support this policy under which the RCMP francophone staff would be reduced from 20.8 to 14.1 per cent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) REDUCTION OF FRANCOPHONE EMPLOYEES (B) POLICY RELATING TO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. Robert de Cotret, has asked me to clear up the issue of Francophone and Anglophone membership in our great Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I would first like to repeat what the President of the Treasury Board said last Thursday in this House, specifically that policy changes proposed by the RCMP have not yet been submitted to his Treasury Board colleagues nor to himself for future consideration. In that respect, he invited his colleague the Sollicitor General to submit to Treasury Board, at the earliest opportunity, the amendments to its official languages policies as planned by the RCMP.
In that respect, according to our information, the Francophone and Anglophone enrolment is not the only item of its internal policies the RCMP intends to amend. This seems to be timely, because active enrolment cannot be separated from the general context of official language use in that important federal agency. We therefore expect the RCMP representations will also include initiatives to improve the situation as regards working languages and language training.
I feel certain the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier will recognize those are important matters that can be improved within the present framework of the Government's current policies. When Treasury Board reviews those documents, after they are submitted, it will be guided in matters of enrolment by Canadian Government policy, which remains equal access to Public Service Employment for all Canadian men and women of both official language groups. This means that opportunities for full enrolment must be exactly the same, both for French and English-speaking Canadians, whatever their ethnic origin or their basic mother tongue. That principle must apply both to hiring and promotions.
Of course, the Treasury Board cannot ignore that the RCMP has to deal with a complex mandate. It works across our vast land in every Canadian province, at the municipal and provincial levels, except in Quebec and Ontario.
In conclusion, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier for giving us this opportunity to clarify an important matter of concern to us all Canadians.
